bio.en: Grant Lee is the co-founder and CEO of Gamma, the profitable AI-powered presentation and website design tool that reached $100M ARR in just over two years with a ~30-person team and is valued at over $2 billion.
bio.zh: Grant Lee 是 Gamma 的联合创始人兼 CEO；Gamma 是一款盈利的 AI 演示与网站设计工具，仅用 30 人左右的团队在两年多内达到 1 亿美元 ARR，估值超 20 亿美元。

summary.en: Grant tells the story of building Gamma as a small, profitable team serving 50M+ users—despite one investor calling it the 'worst idea' he'd ever heard—and how they grew through hands-on influencer marketing, onboarding micro-influencers manually rather than paying for big creators to read scripts. He shares a relentlessly experimental cadence (idea in the morning, live experiment by afternoon, iterate by evening) and why most people wrongly dismiss the presentation category as a real business. The episode is a tactical masterclass in profitable, sustainable AI-startup growth.
summary.zh: Grant 讲述了用一支精干、盈利的团队服务 5000 万以上用户、打造 Gamma 的故事——尽管有投资人说这是他听过“最烂的点子”，以及他们如何通过亲力亲为的影响者营销实现增长：手动 onboard 微影响者，而非花钱让大网红念脚本。他分享了毫不松懈的实验节奏（早上出点子、下午跑实验、晚上迭代），以及为何大多数人都错误地低估了“演示”这个品类能做成大生意。这期节目是关于盈利、可持续的 AI 创业公司增长的战术公开课。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee

You want to be able to have them tell you story but in their voice. You basically give them a script to read, immediately feels like an ad. That product is not connected really to them in any way. You're much better doing the hard thing, which is hard to scale, finding the thousands of micro influencers that have an audience where your product maybe is actually useful. People really trust what they say. That ends up becoming this wildfire that can spread really, really fast.
turns.zh: 最初所有的 influencer，都是我亲自一个个手动邀请的。我会和每一个人开线上会议，让他们理解 Gamma 代表什么、怎么用这个产品。你要让他们用自己的声音讲你的故事。我觉得很多人一想到 influencer 营销，想到的就是那些很火的、有一百万粉丝的大创作者。这是错误的做法。你基本上就是给他们一个剧本照着念，马上就让人感觉像广告。那个产品跟他们之间其实没有任何关联。你更好的做法是去啃那块难啃但难以规模化的骨头——去找成千上万个 micro influencer（微型影响力者），他们的受众群体里，你的产品可能是真的有用。人们真的很信任他们说的话。这最终会变成一场野火，扩散得特别特别快。

We didn't have that strong word of mouth so that the product could just continue growing. (00:10:55): And so we really asked ourselves, okay, what do we need to change? And the answer is we need to fundamentally change everything. It for us almost became this sort of bet the company sort of moment. Because at that point we were running low on runway. We knew we needed to make progress and we didn't really know what could be done. And so we got everyone together. At this point, the team was just over 12 people. And we said, okay, it's going to be all hands on deck. (00:11:22): We are going to do everything we possibly can to make the first 30 seconds of the product feel magical. The moment you land into the product, it has to be great, and it has to be so great that someone that goes through that onboarding is going to tell all their friends. And if we can get that right, then maybe we have a chance at actually doing something in this space. And so we spent three, four months actually after the product launch, we felt great, but we knew we had to go back to the drawing board. (00:11:48): We spent the next three, four months actually revamping the entire onboarding experience. And of course, this is also where AI for us kind of played a big role. We actually rebuilt it so that AI was part of the actual onboarding. So every single new user would experience this sort of magic in the first 30 seconds. And so we relaunched, this is end of March 2023. And all of a sudden, we'd go from a few hundred signups a day to now first day it was like a couple thousand, and then the next day would be like 5,000 signups, and then 10,000 signups a day, and then 20,000 signups a day. (00:12:21): And then it just kept going up. And we weren't doing any sort of marketing, no advertising. It was all sort of organic word of mouth virality of the product, people using the product and sharing it with others, where we for the first time really felt this pull. We didn't have to do anything. Product was just growing. And it was just such a distinct difference between that feeling and coming out of the Product Hunt launch where we could have fooled ourselves into thinking we have product market fit. I think the temptation would've been, hey, let's just spend more on ads or spend more on marketing. Because we'll just fuel the top of the funnel and everything else will work itself out. (00:12:53): I think that would've been a trap. I think that would've led us down to this path of trying to brute force our way into product market fit. And it would just always be sort of a fleeting sort of destination. We would never actually arrive. And so I think we made the tough call, the right call. It was a sort of bet the company moment, and I think on the other side it just felt so different.
turns.zh: 好。我先讲讲我们认为自己可能找到了产品市场契合的那个时刻。我觉得很多创始人会问自己，我们到底有没有找到。而且我觉得人常常会有种诱惑，几乎骗自己相信已经找到了。所以我们做了第一次公开 beta 发布，那是 2022 年 8 月。我们在 Product Hunt 上线，感觉特别好。我们觉得自己发布得很成功，最后拿了当日最佳产品、当周最佳、当月最佳。那一刻就想，哇，我觉得我们手里有点东西了。(00:10:32)：然后我们看注册数，一开始注册量会飙升，然后就平了。我们每天还是有新用户进来，但显然我们没有很强的口碑。没有很强的自然病毒式传播。所以如果我们顺其自然发展下去，我们知道产品不会自己长起来。缺了点什么。我们没有那种强口碑，让产品能持续地自己增长。(00:10:55)：所以我们认真问自己，好，我们需要改什么？答案是，我们得从根本上改变一切。对我们来说，这几乎成了那种“all in 公司”的时刻。因为那时候我们的跑道（runway）已经快见底了。我们知道必须取得进展，但又不知道能做什么。于是我们把所有人聚到一起。当时团队刚过 12 人。我们说，好，全员上阵。(00:11:22)：我们要用尽一切办法，让产品的前 30 秒感觉像魔法一样。你一进产品，体验就必须很棒，而且得好到那种程度——用过这个引导流程的人会去告诉所有朋友。如果我们能把这点做对，那我们或许才有机会在这个领域真正做点事。所以产品发布后，我们其实又花了三、四个月——当时感觉很好，但我们清楚得回到画板上重来。(00:11:48)：接下来的三、四个月，我们彻底重做了整个引导体验。当然，这也是 AI 对我们发挥大作用的地方。我们真的重建了它，让 AI 成为引导流程本身的一部分。于是每个新用户在前 30 秒都能体验到这种魔法。我们重新上线，那是 2023 年 3 月底。突然之间，我们每天从几百个注册涨到——第一天大概几千，第二天五千，然后每天一万，然后每天两万。(00:12:21)：然后就一路往上。我们没做任何营销，没打任何广告。全都是产品自然口碑病毒式的传播，人们用产品然后分享给别人，我们第一次真正感受到了这种拉力。我们什么都不用做，产品自己就在长。这跟 Product Hunt 发布后那种感觉形成了鲜明对比——那时候我们差点骗自己相信已经找到了产品市场契合。当时诱惑可能是，嘿，我们多砸点广告、多砸点营销就行。因为我们只要给漏斗顶部注更多水，其他的自然会解决。(00:12:53)：我觉得那会是个陷阱。那会把我们引向试图用蛮力硬闯出产品市场契合的路，而且那永远只是个稍纵即逝的目的地，我们永远到不了。所以我觉得我们做了艰难但正确的决定。那是种 all in 公司的时刻，而到了另一侧，感觉完全不一样了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Grant, this is exactly what I wanted this conversation to be. I'm so excited. I have so many questions I have to follow up on the stuff you shared before we even get to the rest of the journey. So one is essentially what you're describing is product market fit to you was when organic growth started to really take off, and it was just growing through word of mouth. You weren't doing much because it was so awesome, people were telling their friends about it. Is there anything more there that might be helpful for people to share just to hear about just like, okay, here's what it actually looks like?
turns.zh: Grant，这正是一场对话该有的样子，我太兴奋了。我有太多问题要追问你前面分享的内容，还没到旅程的其余部分呢。首先一点，你描述的“产品市场契合”是：当自然增长真正起飞、靠口碑自己长起来。你没怎么费力，因为它太棒了，人们在跟朋友讲。这方面还有没有更多值得分享的，就是让人听听，好，实际情况是这样的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean my one piece of advice is when you're early on, your mindset should almost be like you're trying to create a word of mouth machine. If you can get that part right, everything else becomes significantly easier. And if you have any, and I think this applies to both prosumer, B2C, as well as even B2B products, if you have a B2B product, even if you're not telling all of your friends, you should be telling colleagues where that product is relevant. You should probably be telling former coworkers where, hey, you've discovered something like, oh, I wish we had this in our prior lives, and that should even be magical. (00:14:14): And then you should see that in all the leads that are coming through or people coming through through your prospects and your existing customers. If you're not seeing a healthy chunk of those leads come through that way, I would go back. I'm like, why? Why is that not happening? Because again, that's the massive tailwind you need where every single thing you do on top of that, all the marketing, all the sales, all the advertising, you're just going to have it becomes way, way easier.
turns.zh: 有。我的一个建议是，早期的时候，你的心态应该几乎像是在打造一台口碑机器。如果你能把这部分做对，其他一切都会容易得多。而且我觉得这对 prosumer（专业消费者）、B2C，甚至 B2B 产品都适用——如果你做的是 B2B 产品，即便你不会告诉所有朋友，你也应该告诉相关的同事。你大概应该告诉前同事，说，嘿，我发现了一个东西，噢，真希望我们以前就有这个，那也应该让人感觉魔法般。(00:14:14)：然后你应该在所有进来的线索、或者你的潜在客户和现有客户里看到这一点。如果你没看到其中有相当大一部分是这么来的，我会回过头想，为什么？为什么没发生？因为再说一遍，这就是你需要的巨大顺风——在此之上你做的每一件事，所有营销、所有销售、所有广告，都会变得容易非常多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much of this was, you described it as a word of mouth machine, how much of this was word of mouth loops and virality features versus just the product itself? One was awesome and two is kind of innately shareable because it's presentations people share with each other.
turns.zh: 你说的“口碑机器”里，有多少是口碑循环和病毒式功能，又有多少纯粹是产品本身？一是它本身就很棒，二是它天然就可分享，因为是演示文稿，人们会互相分享。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think for us, we do benefit from being in a category where, by nature of it, if you like Gamma, you're sharing it, presenting it to others. So I think for us it's a combination of both. And ideally, you have other ways where word of mouth or organic virality can happen in your product. So by nature of usage, like it's being shared. (00:15:09): We basically had an internal mantra that, we go back to the first 30 seconds, we want it to be dead simple for someone to create content, we want to be dead simple for them to share it. And everything we did for that first 30 seconds, or call it the first few minutes, is remove friction so that they can do both of those things. Create and share. And I think other people, when you look at your own product, you think about, okay, what is it about my product and how it gets used? Can you remove friction such that it can actually spread, and even if it's locally within an organization or within a workspace, just be able to enable that as much as you possibly can.
turns.zh: 完全对。我觉得对我们来说，我们确实受益于处在一个品类中——本质上，如果你喜欢 Gamma，你就是在分享它、把它演示给别人看。所以对我们来说两者兼而有之。而且理想情况下，你还有其他方式能让口碑或自然病毒传播在你的产品里发生，由使用本身自然带来，比如它正在被分享。(00:15:09)：我们内部有个信条：回到前 30 秒，我们要让任何人创建内容简单到极致，要让分享简单到极致。我们对那前 30 秒、或者说前几分钟做的一切，都是为了消除摩擦，让他们能同时做这两件事——创建和分享。其他人看自己的产品时，也应该想，好，我的产品是怎么被用的？我能消除摩擦，让它真正能扩散吗？哪怕只是在一个组织内部或一个工作区里，尽可能地去促成这件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other really profound point you're making here is the story of you won product of the day on Product Hunt, which alone is so hard. So many people try to win and don't. Most people don't. I've tried to help companies win, and it's a really hard thing to achieve. And then you won product of the week and product of the month, and still you're like, no, this isn't working. Most people that achieve that are like, no, we got this, and they would not have to bet the company. There wouldn't be a feeling that we have to rethink everything. What is it there that you're just like, no, this isn't going to work, as much as exciting as this is, this isn't it?
turns.zh: 你在这里说的另一个非常深刻的点是：你们在 Product Hunt 上拿了当日最佳产品，这本身就已经极难了。很多人想拿都拿不到。大多数人拿不到。我也帮过公司去拿，那真是个很难达成的事。然后你们还拿了当周最佳、当月最佳，可你还是觉得，不，这不行。大多数达成这个的人会想，不，我们搞定了，他们根本不需要 all in 公司，不会有“我们得重新思考一切”的感觉。你当时是怎么就断定，不，这行不通，再兴奋也不是它？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean part of being a founder is being as self-aware as you can and be your own worst critic. And so oftentimes you want to have these vanity metrics that feel good to celebrate, and you should celebrate. But you should know when it's a vanity metric versus is this core to our growth engine? If this number goes up, does it mean the product is working? And I think that's where we looked at, okay, it felt good to win those things. We kind of put ourselves at least on the map. But it wasn't good enough to actually have this sort of feeling that we had a core growth engine we could just invest in and get better and better. That wasn't there yet.
turns.zh: 是啊，做创始人有一部分就是要尽可能自省，做自己最严厉的批评者。所以你常常会有这些虚荣指标（vanity metrics）想拿来庆祝，而且你应该庆祝。但你要知道什么时候它是虚荣指标，什么时候它是我们增长引擎的核心。如果这个数字涨了，是不是意味着产品在起作用？我们当时就是这么看的：赢了那些奖感觉很好，至少让我们上了地图。但还远不足以让我们产生那种感觉——觉得有了一个核心增长引擎，可以不断投资、越来越好。那个还不存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially it kind of started to just plateau and slow. It wasn't like this rocket ship that took off from that point.
turns.zh: 所以本质上它开始停滞、放缓了。并不是从那刻起就成了一艘起飞的火箭。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, it was still like we were still getting signups. They were coming through. But you could just tell there wasn't this building momentum. And I think that's where it's always hard to tell. You have to, me and my co-founders, we sat down, we're trying to be honest with ourselves. Okay, is this going to be enough? And it just really felt like it wasn't going to be good.
turns.zh: 对，还是那样——我们仍有注册，用户还在进来。但你能感觉到没有那种积聚的势头。我觉得这种时候最难判断。我和我的联合创始人坐下来，试着对自己诚实：好，这就够了吗？而它真的让人感觉不够好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other point here is the power of onboarding, which comes up a bunch on this podcast when you talk about driving retention. So you launched Product Hunt, did great and then started kind of petering out. How much did the product change after things started to work versus onboarding? Just like how important was onboarding? And then just tell us why the first 30 seconds, where'd you come up with that number?
turns.zh: 这里的另一点是引导（onboarding）的力量，这档播客聊留存时经常提到。所以你们上线了 Product Hunt，表现很好，然后开始有点后继乏力。在产品开始奏效之后，产品本身改了多少，相对引导又改了多少？引导到底有多重要？再跟我们说说为什么是前 30 秒，那个数字你是怎么来的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. So for us, the onboarding and the product experience, for us that's intertwined. The analogy I always think about is if you go into a restaurant and maybe the food is good, but when you really think about the user experience, it's like the moment you walk into the door, you get seated, the waitress, waiter comes by, greets you, you can order. And of course the food has to taste good. And then you finally get the bill and you leave. Is that entire experience something that feels delightful? Is it good enough for you to tell your friends about? If someone just came by and dropped the food on your plate on the table, and just left and never came with a bill, I'm like, okay, maybe I'm not going to recommend this to somebody else. (00:18:18): And so for us, we thought about, okay, the first moment someone walks through our door, dropping into the product, what is something we can give them? Can we shorten that time to value as much as possible? A lot of this is inspired by Scott Belsky, he talks about that first mile, the first 15 minutes. And I think that's totally right. And I think one approach is you think about new users as you almost have a cynical view of them. You have to think about them being selfish, vain, and lazy, right? They're coming in, they have no desire to learn a new tool. (00:18:48): And so what can you give them in that first 30 seconds that earns you the next 30 seconds and then the next 30 seconds? And so for us, we knew that if we can't, people's attention span is even shorter to today than maybe 10 years ago, and so what is it in that first 30 seconds, can we actually show you something and earn the right to keep building that relationship with you? We really thought a lot about that, and certainly that's all we could really afford at the time. We only had 12 people building. It's like we couldn't make an entirely revamp the entire product. We knew that we had to least put all of our energy into one spot, and so we made that coming into the door, come through the door, make that moment feel magical so that we can do a little bit more over time.
turns.zh: 对。对我们来说，引导和产品体验是交织在一起的。我常打的比方是：你进一家餐厅，可能菜不错，但你真要衡量用户体验，是从你进门那一刻——有人带你入座，服务员过来打招呼，你可以点单。当然菜得好吃。最后你拿到账单离开。这整个体验让人愉悦吗？好到你会推荐给朋友吗？如果有人就是过来把菜往你桌上一放，然后走了，永远不拿来账单，我就会想，好吧，我大概不会把这推荐给别人。(00:18:18)：所以我们想，好，一个人第一次踏进我们“门”、进入产品的那一刻，我们能给他们什么？我们能不能尽可能缩短“到价值的时间”（time to value）？这很多是受 Scott Belsky 启发，他讲“第一英里”（first mile），也就是前 15 分钟。我觉得那完全对。还有一个思路是，你要带着一种对用户的“愤世嫉俗”的看法去想新用户。你得把他们想成自私、爱虚荣、又懒的——他们进来，根本不想学一个新工具。(00:18:48)：所以那前 30 秒你能给什么，来赢得下一个 30 秒、再下一个 30 秒？对我们来说，我们知道如果我们做不到，人们的注意力比十年前更短，所以在那前 30 秒里，我们能给你看点什么，赢得继续和你建立关系的权利？我们真的想了很多。而且那也确实是我们当时唯一负担得起的。我们只有 12 个人在做产品。我们不可能把整个产品彻底重做。我们知道至少得把全部精力放到一个点上，所以我们选了进门那个瞬间——让人进来的那一刻感觉像魔法，这样我们以后能慢慢做更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love your point about how you could think of it as like, okay, it's onboarding versus the product. The lens of how do we make this incredibly valuable and aha-ish for the first 30 seconds almost informs what the product should be.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你说的这点——你怎么把它看成“是引导还是产品”的二分，其实换个镜头想“我们怎么让前 30 秒极其有价值、有 aha 感”，这几乎反过来定义了产品应该是什么。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. It really helps you pull forward what is the most magical thing about your product. Sometimes founders will think about the five, 10 features. Well, maybe there's only one thing that kind of differentiates you. I try to learn a lot from, we'll get into some of the marketing pieces of this, but even just having this sort of founder led marketing lens of what can I do to help a new user just understand. There's this thing from consumer advertising, which is you throw a consumer one egg, they can probably catch it. You throw them four or five eggs, they're probably going to drop all of them. (00:20:12): And oftentimes founders want to talk about the four or five features they have, maybe 10 features. And then the consumer is totally confused, like why do I need this thing? We try to just give them that one egg, that one first experience. We're like, okay, create a slide in seconds. That's the egg. I'm going to throw you this egg. Is that compelling to you? Some people are still going to opt out, but for the people that catch that, you're solving a real problem for them, and then you can continue building on that over time. You've given them enough so that they'll sit around and keep playing with your product.
turns.zh: 对。它真的帮你把“产品最魔法的那一点”拉到前面。有时创始人会想着那五六个、十个功能。但也许真正让你与众不同的只有一件事。我试着从很多地方学——后面会聊到一些营销的东西——但就算只是带着创始人主导营销的视角去想，我能为新用户做什么、让他们一下子就懂。消费广告里有个说法：你扔给消费者一个鸡蛋，他大概接得住；你扔四五个，他大概全掉地上。(00:20:12)：而创始人常常想讲自己四五个、甚至十个功能。消费者就完全懵了：我为什么要这东西？我们尽量只给他们那一个鸡蛋，那第一次的体验。我们想，好，几秒钟做出一张幻灯片。那就是那个鸡蛋。我扔给你这个鸡蛋。你觉得有吸引力吗？还是会有人不买账，但接住的人，你是在真正解决他们的问题，然后你可以随着时间继续往上建。你已经给了他们足够的东西，让他们留下来继续玩你的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a hilarious metaphor I've never heard for onboarding time to value, just focus on one egg at a time. Just going even further back, what was the original insight that you had that led to Gamma and what Gamma is today?
turns.zh: 这个关于引导“到价值时间”的比喻我从来没听过，笑死，就是一次专注一个鸡蛋。再往回退一点，当初是什么原始洞察催生了 Gamma 和今天的 Gamma？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: After the last startup I was at was acquired, I went back into kind of my roots, which is consulting. I was advising early stage startups. And the sort of medium I was using was Google Slides. So I just remember this late night trying to prepare for next day's meeting, trying to format and figure out the right layout, and spending hours just trying to get the sort of look and feel right, rather than the content itself. And for me, that just felt completely backwards. I should be spending 90% of the time on the content, 10% maybe on the design and formatting. (00:21:25): And so the question just was what if there's a better way? What if we could reimagine this format from the ground up? Slides have been around for almost 40 years as the default medium of choice for a lot of this. And so we thought about, okay, if we had different building blocks, different primitives, so you're not locked into the fixed 16 by nine slide, what could we offer to users? And so that was really the starting point of all this.
turns.zh: 我上一家创业公司被收购后，我回到我的老本行——咨询。我当时在给早期创业公司做顾问，用的媒介是 Google Slides。我记得有天深夜，我为了准备第二天的会，一直在调格式、找合适的排版，花了好几个小时就为了让外观感觉对，而不是内容本身。对我来说，那感觉完全本末倒置。我应该把 90% 的时间花在内容上，10% 也许花在设计排版上。(00:21:25)：所以问题就是：如果有更好的方式呢？如果我们能从零重新构想这个格式呢？幻灯片作为很多人默认的媒介已经快 40 年了。所以我们想，好，如果我们有不同的构建模块、不同的基元（primitives），你就不会被锁死在固定的 16:9 幻灯片里，我们能给用户什么？那就是这一切真正的起点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hearing this, I could see why investors would be like, I guess so. But slides has been around, PowerPoint has been around 40 years. I get it. I get why people would be... And specifically AI, was that a part of the vision initially, or did AI start to come up, and then wow, great timing,
turns.zh: 听你这么说，我能理解为什么投资人会那样了。但幻灯片已经存在，PowerPoint 都 40 年了。我懂。我懂为什么人们会……尤其 AI，那一开始是愿景的一部分吗，还是 AI 后来才出现，然后哇，时机太好了——

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Great timing. It wasn't part of the original vision, although the spirit was there, which is we wanted to make it incredibly fast and effortless for people to create content. So it just so happened that AI was a magical gift that allowed us to do all those things along the same sort of ambition or vision that we had. And so we integrated it core to all the building blocks we were already building well before AI was part of the picture.
turns.zh: 时机太好了。它本来不是原始愿景的一部分，但精神在——我们想让人们创建内容快到极致、毫不费力。所以 AI 恰好是一份魔法礼物，让我们能沿着原本的野心和愿景去做所有这些事。所以我们在 AI 成为话题之前很久，就已经把它整合进我们一直在搭建的所有构建模块的核心里了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a cool other example. There's just so many examples of ideas that were not possible before are now very possible with AI. And it's a great opportunity for people to come after as these places, categories, people think is an impossible place to build a big business. AI now allows it. Awesome. (00:22:43): Speaking of that, let's talk about the growth journey, and how you actually grew from nothing to 100 million ARR in just over two years. I'm thinking we break it up. I know these milestones aren't that clear, but kind of like zero to 100 million ARR, one to 10, 10 to 100, something like that. And let's just see how it goes. How did you get your first set of users? How'd you get your, say, first 100 users? How'd you get to 100 million ARR from zero?
turns.zh: 这又是一个超酷的例子。太多以前不可能的想法，现在靠 AI 变得可能了。对人们来说，去进攻那些大家以为“根本做不出大生意”的品类和领域，是个巨大的机会。AI 现在让它成为可能。太棒了。(00:22:43)：说到这里，我们聊聊增长之旅，以及你们怎么在两年多里从零做到 1 亿美元 ARR。我想我们分一下阶段。我知道这些里程碑没那么清晰，但大概是零到 1 亿 ARR，或者一档到十档、十档到一百档这种。我们就看怎么走。你们怎么拿到第一批用户的？比如头 100 个用户怎么来的？又怎么从零到 1 亿 ARR 的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Our first 100 looks very different, I'd say. So this was even pre this sort of AI launch we had. The first 100 users for a product like ours, you're trying to convince all your friends to use the product. Anybody that's ever made a slide deck, you're trying to talk to. And I think early on, your friends want to do you a favor, so they're going to try the product. They're also going to lie to you. They're going to tell you how great it is. And then you look at the usage and nobody's coming back. (00:23:33): And so I think our first 100 was sort of gradually hard-earned post the product launch, people learning like, okay, this is kind of becoming a little bit more useful. Usage was still pretty episodic, so they weren't coming back every week. And then I do think the moment post the AI launch is where all of a sudden we saw that sort of organic growth happening, people coming back to the product regularly. And so that's where, it wasn't even the first hundred, it was like probably the first 10,000 users all came within a pretty short time period after that initial launch.
turns.zh: 我们头 100 个用户，我得说，非常不一样。那甚至还在我们那次 AI 发布之前。像我们这样的产品，头 100 个用户就是你试图说服所有朋友用。任何做过幻灯片的人，你都去聊。我觉得早期你朋友想给你个面子，所以会试产品。然后他们也会骗你。他们会告诉你多棒。然后你一看使用数据，没一个人回来。(00:23:33)：所以我觉得我们头 100 个用户，是在产品发布后一点点辛苦攒出来的，人们慢慢觉得，好吧，这开始有点用了。使用还是挺零星，所以不是每周都回来。然后我觉得 AI 发布之后那个时刻，我们才突然看到那种自然增长发生了，人们定期回到产品。所以那甚至不是头一百个——大概是头一万个用户，全都在那次初始发布后相当短的时间内涌进来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to talk about monetization pricing later, which is obviously an important part of actual getting to million ARR and 10 million AAR. So what I'm hearing essentially is the Product Hunt launch was a big part of just the first 10,000-ish users. I know there was also a tweet when you relaunched that helped in a big way. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 棒。我们晚点会聊变现和定价，那显然是真正做到 100 万 ARR 和 1000 万 ARR 的重要部分。所以我听下来，Product Hunt 发布基本贡献了头一万个左右的用户。我知道你们重新发布时还有一条推文帮了大忙。说说那个。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. So when we did our AI launch, we didn't do our AI launch on Product Hunt. We basically said, hey, let's just put it out on Twitter, see if we can get some virality. And honestly, we kind came up with kind of a clickbaity sort of tweet. It was like the most valuable skill in business is about to become obsolete. And so it was intentional in that we wanted to create a little bit of engagement. We knew that having sort of a more provocative in a tweet would allow people to engage with it. (00:24:54): And so after a couple of days, all of a sudden it started getting a little bit more viral and a lot more engagement. And we looked and it was basically because Paul Graham had commented and saying something like, "Surely, the thing that the slide deck is describing is more valuable than the slide itself." And obviously it was fun just to see that comment. I think once that comment came through, even more engagement on the post. And then that was really the whole intent of that post was just to be able to have that level of engagement so that people, it would have some level of reach. (00:25:24): And so for me, it was almost like my first learning moment, going back to what does founder led marketing even mean? It means how do you actually break through the noise? How do you get a chance to have people even engage with a post like that? Part of that is copywriting, part of that is storytelling. Part of that is just having even the right visuals to share. And so it was for me kind of a moment just understanding, hey, to kind of do this right, you kind of have to do things that maybe you're not super comfortable with, but it makes a difference.
turns.zh: 好。我们做 AI 发布时，没在 Product Hunt 上发。我们基本想，嘿，就发到 Twitter 上，看能不能有点病毒传播。老实说，我们有点故意写了条标题党推文。大概是“商业里最有价值的技能马上要过时了”。这是有意的，我们想制造一点互动。我们知道一条更挑衅的推文能让人们参与进来。(00:24:54)：过了几天，它突然开始更有病毒传播、互动更多了。我们一看，基本是因为 Paul Graham 评论了一句，大意是：“当然，幻灯片所描述的东西，比幻灯片本身更有价值。”看到那条评论本身就很有趣。我觉得那条评论一出，帖子互动更多了。而那其实就是那条帖子的全部目的——能有那样的互动量级，让帖子有一定触达。(00:25:24)：所以对我来说，那几乎是我第一个学习时刻，回到“创始人主导营销到底是什么意思”这个问题。它意味着你怎么真正突破噪音？你怎么获得机会让人去互动这样一条帖子？一部分是文案，一部分是讲故事，一部分就是有对的视觉素材去分享。所以对我而言，那是个理解“嘿，要把这事做对，你得做一些可能自己不太舒服、但确实有用的事”的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a fun story. So you intentionally set that announcement up to be controversial is what I'm hearing?
turns.zh: 太好玩了。所以我听到的是，你故意把那条公告设计得有争议？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah. I'd say provocative. A little spicy.
turns.zh: 完全对。我会说是挑衅，有点刺激。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool. So essentially you got to 10,000 users through Product Hunt, and then essentially one controversial tweet that ended up baiting Paul Graham to comment.
turns.zh: 太酷了。所以本质上你们通过 Product Hunt 到了一万个用户，然后靠一条有争议的推文，最后把 Paul Graham 钓出来评论。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And it was just a comment. It wasn't even him retweeting it.
turns.zh: 厉害。而且就只是个评论，他甚至没转推。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: No, just a comment. And then others would pile on.
turns.zh: 没有，就只是个评论。然后别人会跟着涌进来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's interesting how much a comment can increase the distribution of a tweet versus them retweeting it or quote tweeting it.
turns.zh: 对。一条评论能多大程度提升一条推文的传播，相比转推或者引用推文，挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. And of course the algorithm change all the time. So part of it was just luck based on when it happened, how it happened, who posted.
turns.zh: 完全对。当然算法一直在变。所以一部分纯粹是运气——取决于什么时候发生、怎么发生、谁发的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you use this term founder led marketing, which I love, and I'm already seeing it in action here. This is you thinking about, it's not delegating to someone in marketing, it's not hiring an agency, it's like how do I tell a story that I think will break through the noise based on you building this company, having the insight to build this product. And I guess is there anything more there you think is important for people to hear about the importance of the founder thinking through this stuff?
turns.zh: 你用了“创始人主导营销”这个词，我很喜欢，而且我在这里已经看到它在发挥作用了。就是你自己在想——不是委托给营销部门的人，不是雇个代理公司，而是“我怎么讲一个我觉得能突破噪音的故事”，基于你创办这家公司、有做这个产品的洞察。我想还有没有什么更重要的，想让大家听到关于创始人为何要亲自想这些事？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think most people today are probably familiar with founder-led sales, which is still very, very important. I think before you hire your first salesperson or AE, it's great for the founder to understand what it takes. And they're going to craft the right narrative, the right story. At my previous role, I was the COO at a startup where I was doing a lot of, I wasn't founder, but I was early. And so I was helping the founders go through this, and really helping go into meetings with a client or a prospect and saying, "Hey, this is why our product is interesting." (00:27:26): And I think today there's so many AI startups that are much more either B2C or prosumer. And so you're not necessarily talking to individual prospects, but the idea that you can be really in control of the narrative on the marketing side is really, really important. And I think I'll describe a few things where, over time, I think that skill set just really, really helps you. (00:27:48): One is you have a chance to be a creator yourself these days. I think a lot of founders are trying to be more active on social media. And I think if you can kind of overcome the initial cringe factor of seeing yourself and postings like, oh, this doesn't feel authentic, if you can overcome that initial feeling, you start investing into like, okay, how do I become a better copywriter? How do I articulate something that is clear, not just clever? I think there's that saying where obviously if you can have that clarity, that's super important. And most people will try to get super creative with their copywriting, but that's not usually the right way to break through and communicate something. So how do you improve your own copywriting? (00:28:27): And then that allows you to actually have a higher bar when you start working with other marketers, or in this case for us, working with influencers. If you're working with influencers and creators, and you can totally empathize with how they approach that work, and you know what a good hook looks like or you know how to structure a good post, you can only do that if you've gone through it a little bit yourself and you know how hard it is. And I think too many founders will then just say, they'll write something that just feels so much like an ad, and then they'll give it to a creator to help amplify. And then that just never works. And so I do think part of founder-led marketing is going through this yourself.
turns.zh: 有。我觉得今天大多数人可能都熟悉“创始人主导销售”（founder-led sales），那仍然非常重要。我觉得在你招第一个销售或 AE 之前，创始人最好先搞清楚那需要什么。他们会打磨出对的故事、对的叙述。我上一份工作是一家创业公司的 COO，我做了很多——我不是创始人，但我很早期。所以我帮创始人走过这个过程，真的进到和客户或潜在客户的会里说：“嘿，这就是我们产品有意思的地方。”(00:27:26)：我觉得今天很多 AI 创业公司更偏 B2C 或 prosumer。所以你不一定在跟单个潜在客户谈，但你能真正掌控营销侧叙事的这个想法，真的非常重要。我会描述几件事，随着时间，我觉得那套技能真的真的帮到你。(00:27:48)：一是现在你有机会自己成为创作者。我觉得很多创始人都想在社交媒体上更活跃。如果你能克服最初看到自己发东西时那种“起鸡皮疙瘩”的感觉——噢，这不真实——克服那最初的感觉后，你会开始投入：好，我怎么成为更好的文案写手？我怎么把一个东西讲清楚，而不只是讲得巧妙？有句话说，显然如果你能做到清晰，那就超级重要。大多数人会试图把文案写得太有创意，但那通常不是突破噪音、传达信息的正确方式。那你怎么提升自己的文案？(00:28:27)：然后这会让你在和其他营销人合作时——对我们来说，是和 influencer 合作时——有更高的标准。如果你和 influencer、创作者合作，你能完全共情他们怎么做这工作，你知道一个好的钩子（hook）长什么样、你知道怎么组织一条好帖子，只有你自己也稍微走过一遍、知道这有多难，你才能做到。太多创始人会直接写那种感觉超像广告的东西，然后丢给创作者去放大。那永远没用。所以我觉得创始人主导营销的一部分，就是你自己走过这个过程。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: And so I do think part of founder-led marketing is going through this yourself, using your own platform. In the beginning it's probably going to be super small. But as you get bigger, you have a platform to ... You have a voice and people listen. And you're going to get better and better at your own storytelling. I think these are all skills you should invest in as early as possible, because you know you're going to have to get better and better. It's like practice, you got to practice over and over.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得创始人主导营销的一部分，就是你自己走过这个过程，用你自己的平台。一开始它可能超级小。但你变大后，你就有了一个平台去……你有声音，有人听。你会越来越会讲自己的故事。我觉得这些都是你应该尽早投资的技能，因为你知道你必定会越来越好。就像练习，你得一遍遍练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely want to pull on this thread more because you tweeting the lessons you learned building Gamma is what led to this conversation. I was reading, I'm like, " Okay, he's sharing a bunch of stuff, but there's so much more I want to hear." And we're going to talk through this and go in a lot more depth than what you've shared on Twitter. But I love that that's example of that working, having this conversation. (00:29:41): So let me ask a couple of questions here. One is just how do you find time as a founder or CEO of a very fast growing crazy startup? We have so much to do. How do you just allocate the time to do this? And then any just key lessons you've learned about doing this well, beyond what you've already shared for people that want to try to start sharing things on LinkedIn and Twitter?
turns.zh: 我一定要顺着这条线多拉一点，因为你发那些“做 Gamma 学到的经验”的推文，才促成了这场对话。我当时读着，心想“好吧，他分享了一堆东西，但我还有太多想听的”。我们这场会把你推特上分享过的东西讲得更深。但我喜欢这就是那个方法奏效的例子，促成了这场对话。(00:29:41)：所以让我问几个问题。一是作为一个飞速增长、忙疯了的创业公司的创始人或 CEO，你怎么挤出时间？我们有太多事要做。你怎么分配时间去做这个？然后，除了你已经分享的，对想在 LinkedIn 和 Twitter 上开始分享的人，有没有什么关键经验？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: My advice is definitely just to try to start small. Don't let it become so intimidating that you just don't get started. For me, it was like just having a notepad or a Google Doc around in the beginning where I would just constantly jot down, okay, this is something I learned or something I observed or something that worked well, something that was unintuitive but worked, and just start creating a log of that. And then once I had enough of those, and I'd spend basically every week, I'd block off a few hours to go a little bit deeper. I'd take a lot of those bullet points and try to say, "Is there enough here to turn this into maybe a post or something that can be shared broadly?" And in the beginning I didn't have enough. It was all sort of scattered thoughts. But over time you start accumulating some interesting themes. And then I would start stress testing some of that. (00:30:45): So I would tell my teammates like, "Hey, this is something interesting. Do you find this interesting?" And if there were enough like, "Oh yeah, I would not have expected that", or, "That's not something I've ever heard before," then I'd actually start crafting the initial post. And then you actually just put it out there. I think what I've learned is, even for LinkedIn versus Twitter, the audiences want different things. And so you almost have to then have different tones of voices or even nuggets or sharing. For me, I invested much more in LinkedIn early on just because it felt a little bit more natural for me. And then over time I said, "Okay, well I'm going to start packaging certain content for Twitter that's actually different than what I would post on LinkedIn." Sometimes on Twitter you get even more tactical or even more into the weeds. And so I found that to be helpful. (00:31:27): But honestly, I'm still learning. And so every time you post, you go back, after a couple of weeks you go and say, "Okay, what things are actually being engaged with? Are things actually creating ..." Ideally you're creating enough value where people are either bookmarking it, sharing it, retweeting it, these things that are signals for there's something valuable there. And then you just go back and you start collecting your own sort of, these are my all-star posts, these are the ones that I've actually broken through. And then you go back and try to understand, okay, what about that post do I think was actually useful? Was it the actual content? Was it the structure of the content? Was it some sort of contrarian advice? And you start thematically bunching that together such that as you're brainstorming every week, you just have a good sort of body of work to work off.
turns.zh: 我的建议绝对是先从小处开始。别让它变得吓人以至于你根本不开始。对我来说，一开始就是有个记事本或 Google Doc，我不断随手记：好，这是我学到的、观察到的、管用的、反直觉但有用的东西，开始建一个这样的日志。等攒够了，我基本每周会空出几个小时钻深一点。我把那些要点拿出来，试着说：“这里够不够，能变成一篇可以广泛分享的帖子？”一开始不够，都是零散想法。但随着时间你会积累出一些有意思的主题。然后我会开始测试。(00:30:45)：我会跟队友说：“嘿，这东西有意思。你觉得有意思吗？”如果有足够多的人说“噢对，我没想到这个”，或者“我从没听过这个”，那我才真的开始打磨初稿。然后你就发出去。我学到的是，哪怕 LinkedIn 和 Twitter，受众想要的东西也不同。所以你几乎得用不同的语调、甚至不同的小料去分享。我早期在 LinkedIn 上投入多得多，因为对我更自然。然后随着时间我再说：“好，我要开始为 Twitter 专门打包一些内容和 LinkedIn 上发的不同。”有时 Twitter 上你会更实操、更钻细节。我觉得这很有帮助。(00:31:27)：但老实说，我还在学。所以每次发完，过几周你回去看：好，哪些东西真的有人互动？真的在产生……理想是你创造了足够价值，让人收藏、分享、转推——这些是“这里有有价值东西”的信号。然后你回去开始收集你自己的“全明星帖子”，就是那些真正突破了噪音的。然后你回过头试图理解：好，那篇帖子到底什么有用？是内容本身？是内容结构？是某种反直觉的建议？你开始按主题把它们归类，这样每周头脑风暴时，你就有了一堆好素材可用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting and valuable. So let me mirror back a few of the lessons that I heard here that I think is easy for people to miss. So one is just what to share. What I heard here, and I completely agree with this, and this is what I try to do, is pay attention to things you've learned, things that you find interesting, things that are unintuitive to you. Just have a doc and just put these there. And every time you learn something, find something interesting, just add it to the doc. Or yeah, I haven't heard before is a good one too. (00:32:39): So it's essentially just like if you find it interesting, people on social media will also find it interesting. And one approach is just share it as it's happening, which is what I try to do. Just like, "Oh hey, just learned this thing with with clock code. Check it out." Or save it up for a big long post. The other interesting, I've never heard this before, of post different things to LinkedIn and Twitter. I just copy and paste the same thing. I love that you do something different for the two platforms.
turns.zh: 这太有意思也太有用了。让我把听到的几个容易被人忽略的经验镜像回给你。一是“分享什么”。我听到的是——而且我完全同意，也是我努力做的——留意你学到的、觉得有意思的、对你反直觉的东西。就开个文档放那里。每次你学到什么、发现什么有意思，就加进去。或者“我以前没听过”也是个好标准。(00:32:39)：所以本质上就是：如果你觉得有意思，社交媒体上的人也会觉得有意思。一种做法是边发生边分享，这也是我努力做的。就像“噢嘿，刚跟 clock 团队学到这个，来看看”。或者攒着发一篇大长文。另一个有意思的、我从没听过的——给 LinkedIn 和 Twitter 发不同的东西。我都是直接复制粘贴同一条。我喜欢你为两个平台做不同的东西。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I think we all kind of have intuition that there's just different audiences, right? And so if you know that kind of fundamentally, then the question is how do you package up the story the right way so that the audience is ready to receive it? And I think this can differ by the type of creator or the founder, whoever's posting it, and of course the actual content itself. And so for me, I'm still tweaking, but I do find that just copy and pasting from one to the other doesn't usually work. You almost need to be in the right mindset of, okay, what do I think will be more engaging on Twitter? And then what do I think will be more engaging on LinkedIn? And then test a bunch, see what actually works. Go back and iterate a little bit.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们都有种直觉，就是受众不同，对吧？所以如果你根本上知道这点，问题就是怎么把故事打包对，让受众准备好接收？我觉得这因创作者或创始人类型、当然也因内容本身而异。所以我还在调，但我确实发现直接复制粘贴从一个到另一个通常不行。你几乎得进入对的 mindset：好，Twitter 上什么会更吸引人？LinkedIn 上什么会更吸引人？然后大量测试，看什么真的管用。回去迭代一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you had one bullet point tip for what works on Twitter versus LinkedIn, you shared maybe more tactical on Twitter, is there anything more there you can share?
turns.zh: 所以如果你用一句话总结 Twitter 和 LinkedIn 上什么管用，你说了 Twitter 可能更实操，还有没有什么更多能分享的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, that's what I've found is tactical, oftentimes more contrarian on Twitter. And also I would say technical too. People really like to know, again, going back to getting into the weeds, is this something I feel like I could replicate? And I'm not going to give you ... There's no credibility if you just give a blanket statement or something that feels generic. I really need to know, if you could show me the metrics, even better. I feel like that ... (00:34:22): Versus LinkedIn, it's oftentimes more even just either more aspirational or aspirational or a topic or a theme that just feels relevant at that point in time. And you can just kind of make more of a broader statement. It doesn't need to be as tactical. It's more like inspirational, is like, "Oh, okay, now I need to go and learn a little bit more about pricing and packaging," for instance. And that could be the sort of spark that somebody needs. And you don't need to spell it completely out. Part of it's also that on LinkedIn you can't really do threads. And so doing a super long form post isn't as practical. Maybe that changes in the future, where maybe the tactical pieces, that element might actually change.
turns.zh: 有。我发现的是，Twitter 上更实操、常常更反直觉。而且我也会说更技术。人们真的想知道——回到钻细节——这事我能不能复制？如果你只给一句空泛的话或感觉通用的东西，那没有可信度。我真得知道，如果你能给我看指标，更好。我觉得那……(00:34:22)：相对 LinkedIn，常常更偏鼓舞人心、或者一个当下相关的主题。你可以做更宽泛的陈述，不需要那么实操。更像是启发，比如“噢，好，我现在得去多学点定价和打包”。那可能就是某人需要的一点火花。你不需要全讲透。一部分也是 LinkedIn 上你做不了线程（thread），所以发超长文不现实。也许未来会变，那时候实操内容那部分可能真的会变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And last piece is you said you just block off time. Is there a specific time of the week you do this? How do you actually ... Because everyone's like, "Oh sure, I'll block off time. And then, I don't know, okay, but I actually got to do all this other stuff so I'm not going to use it this time or maybe next week."
turns.zh: 最后一点是你说的你就是空出时间。你一周有特定时间做这个吗？你具体怎么……因为每个人都说“噢当然，我会空出时间。然后，我不知道，噢但我其实得做所有这些别的事，所以这周不做了，也许下周吧。”

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: For me, it's usually two times of the day, very first thing in the morning and last thing at night. And partly it's because of kids. It's almost like I need time where there's just zero distraction and there's no noise in the house, and so I can actually think. And then I think in the mornings it's about where are you finding inspiration, what are topics you're energized by? And then I think at night it's about reflection. What are the things you actually went through that day? You can almost pull up your calendar and be like, "Okay, I talked to X, Y and Z people. And was there anything from those conversations that might be relevant?" That's where I write some of those things. It's more of a recap of actually what happened.
turns.zh: 对我来说，是一天里两个时段：大清早和深夜。一部分是因为孩子。几乎就是我需要一段零干扰、家里没噪音的时间，这样我才能真正思考。早上我关注的是：你在哪找灵感、哪些话题让你有干劲？晚上则是反思：那天你到底经历了什么？你几乎可以翻开日历想：“好，我聊了 X、Y、Z 这几个人。那些对话里有没有什么相关的？”有些东西就是那样写的，更像是实际发生的事的复盘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what helps me to not feel like this is some cringey self-promo egotistical stuff is just it's useful stuff that I've learned that ends up being helpful to people. And people in the comments are always just like, "Oh, that is really cool and useful. Thank you." It's not like self-promotion-
turns.zh: 能让我不觉得这是那种尴尬的自我推销、自大东西的，就是：这都是我学到的、对人有用的东西。评论区的人总是说“噢，这真的酷而且有用。谢谢”。这不是自我推销——

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... it's not just like, "Look how amazing I am. Check out my amazing products." Like, "Here's a thing I learned. You might find it useful."
turns.zh: ……它不是那种“看我多厉害，来看看我超棒的产品”，而是“这是我学到的一个东西，你可能觉得有用”。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: That's exactly right. I think one way of thinking about it, with founder-led sales, it's always about exchange of value, right? You want to be able to give the customer this feeling that they're getting an amazing product. In exchange they're going to pay you money for it. I think with founder-led marketing, it's almost this mindset of you want to give people a ton of content, maybe it's a value in the content, so you're sharing something, maybe some secret tactic or you're giving them something where inherently there's value in it, and in exchange you sort of get goodwill back. You're not necessarily getting money back, you get goodwill. They're going to follow you, they're going to engage with your post, they're going to tell others about it. And then over time you can exchange maybe some of that goodwill for actually talking about my product and announcing it and they're going to help amplify the news. And I think that's magic, where you kind of bank the goodwill for a long period of time by providing just a ton of value with no expectation of anything immediately in return.
turns.zh: 完全对。我想一种思路是：创始人主导销售，永远是关于价值交换，对吧？你想给客户一种感觉——他们在得到一个超棒的产品，作为交换他们会付你钱。我觉得创始人主导营销，几乎是一种 mindset：你想给人们大量内容，也许是内容里的价值，所以你在分享某样东西，也许是某个秘密战术，或者你给他们的东西本身就内含价值，作为交换你多少收获一些善意（goodwill）。你不一定收回钱，你收回善意。他们会关注你、会互动你的帖子、会告诉别人。然后随着时间，你可以用其中一些善意去真正谈你的产品、做发布，他们会帮你放大消息。我觉得那很魔法——你通过长期提供大量价值、不期待任何立即回报，把善意存进“银行”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The book I always point people to when they're struggling with this sort of thing and like, "Okay, I did this and no one cared, didn't do any good," is there's a book by Scott Pressfield, I think is his name, called Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit, which is exactly what is right. Nobody wants to read it. The bar for people to care is very high. There's so much stuff to read and process. And so this book gives you a really good lens of just like, okay, the bar is very high and nobody wants to read your shit, so you have to try really hard to make it really good.
turns.zh: 当人们为这种事挣扎、觉得“好吧，我做了，没人理，没用”时，我总是指给他们一本书，是 Scott Pressfield（我想是这名）写的，叫《没人想读你那堆破烂》（Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit），说的就是这个。没人想读你的东西。人们去在意你的门槛很高。有太多东西要读、要处理。这本书给你一个很好的镜头：门槛很高，没人想读你的破烂，所以你必须非常努力让它真的好。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Great reminder.
turns.zh: 很好的提醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll link to that in the show notes. Okay, let's come back to the growth of Gamma. So we've talked about how you got your first tens of thousands of users, essentially product hunts, rethinking, onboarding, making it really magical, and then this very controversial tweet that Paul Graham commented, created some buzz. Let's talk about the next phase and maybe, I don't know, tell us kind of the ARR at that point through 100 million. Just broadly, what should we know?
turns.zh: 我们会在 shownotes 里放链接。好，回到 Gamma 的增长。我们聊了你怎么拿到头几万用户——基本上是 Product Hunt、重新思考引导、让它真的像魔法，然后那条很有争议、Paul Graham 评论、制造了一些声量的推文。我们聊聊下一阶段，也许说说那时到 1 亿 ARR 之间的 ARR。大致上我们应该知道什么？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: So when we got to about 10 million in ARR, I think there was this feeling for me, which was we knew we needed ways to help just continue to amplify and spread the word about Gamma. I think it was already working in terms of the organic virality was there, and so we did feel like it was time to start amplifying some of this. And I think the main blocker of my mind that I started feeling was that our initial brand was holding us back. And I think a lot of people will discount whether or not a rebrand is valuable. And I think sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. (00:38:39): For us, there's a few different things we looked at. So one, our initial brand was almost more of a placeholder brand because we created it the moment we incorporated the company, which was again late 2020, beginning of 2021, where we needed something so that as we built, we could at least share it with people. We could put up a landing page and just feel like, okay, there's something here. But we didn't invest a whole lot into it. And so it was pretty limited in sort of what I call the DNA of the brand. There wasn't that many ... The art direction was very limited in scope. There wasn't much when it came to voice and tone. (00:39:12): And so it was something that we knew was good enough to start, but it wasn't scalable. And when I think about something that could be scalable, it's almost like you can take the ingredients of a brand and replicate it a ton, this DNA is something where you can imagine creating tons of content around and all feeling pretty cohesive. And I think that needs to be done by design. You're really being thoughtful about every single element. Like what is the art direction you want to go with? What is the voice and tone? Such that as you're creating thousands of pieces of copy, it all feels pretty cohesive. (00:39:45): And so we went back to the drawing board and we spent many months rethinking what would be the brand, what is this vision that we have longer term? Our creative director internally partner with Smith & Diction, an amazing agency that has helped folks like Perplexity also do their rebrand or their initial brand. And we [inaudible 00:40:05] many months just really trying to craft what we think is the core DNA of the brand, and doing so in a way that we could replicate it as much as possible. (00:40:15): Replication piece of it comes into play, because as you start scaling you're going to have to create a ton of content, your own content on social media, ads for performance marketing, assets for influencers to be able to use and showcase in their content. And so you're going from tiny pieces of content to all of a sudden every week we're testing thousands of pieces of creative. And you cannot do that if you don't feel confident that as you're replicating, you have that sort of cohesive feel. So for us that we realized it was going to be necessary and it's why we invested so much. It ended up being way more expensive, way more time consuming than I would've imagined. But I think coming on the other side of it being the right investment, feeling that that was the right time to do it.
turns.zh: 当我们到大概 1000 万 ARR 时，我有一种感觉：我们知道需要一些方式来继续放大、传播 Gamma 的声音。我觉得自然病毒传播那时已经在起作用了，所以我们确实觉得是时候开始放大其中一些了。而当时我脑子里开始觉得的主要阻碍是，我们最初的品牌在拖后腿。很多人会低估一次 rebrand（品牌重塑）到底有没有价值。我觉得有时有，有时没有。(00:38:39)：对我们来说，我们看了几件事。一是我们最初的品牌几乎更像个占位品牌，因为那是我们在成立公司的那一刻创的——又是 2020 年底、2021 年初——我们需要点东西，这样在搭建时至少能分享给别人。我们能放个落地页，感觉“好吧，这里有东西了”。但我们没投入太多。所以它在品牌的“DNA”上相当有限。艺术方向（art direction）范围很窄。在声音和语调（voice and tone）上也没多少。(00:39:12)：所以我们清楚它够起步，但不能扩展。而我想到能扩展的东西，几乎像你能拿品牌的配料大量复制，这个 DNA 是你能想象围绕它造出海量内容、而且都感觉很 cohesive（统一）的。而这需要有意设计。你对每个元素都很用心。比如你想要什么艺术方向？什么声音和语调？这样当你在造几千条文案时，全都感觉很统一。(00:39:45)：所以我们回到画板，花了几个月重新想品牌会是什么、我们更长期的愿景是什么？我们的创意总监在内部和 Smith & Diction 合作——一家很棒的代理公司，也帮过 Perplexity 做 rebrand 或初始品牌。我们[听不清 00:40:05]花了几个月真的在打磨我们认为的品牌核心 DNA，而且是以一种能尽可能复制它的方式。(00:40:15)：复制这一点很重要，因为你一开始扩展，就得造海量内容——你自己在社交媒体上的内容、效果广告（performance marketing）用的广告、给 influencer 用来在他们内容里展示的素材。所以你从一点点内容，突然变成每周我们在测试几千个创意。如果你不确信复制时能有那种统一感，你做不到。所以对我们来说，我们意识到这是必要的，这也是为什么我们投入那么多。它最后比我想象贵得多、耗时得多。但到了另一侧，我觉得是笔对的投入，觉得那是对的时间做这事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how many things you did that feel like this will not work out. Building a startup within the presentation space, doing a whole rebrand in the middle of scaling, also just reworking the entire product after you launched and just rethinking the whole thing. All these things and everyone's always like, "No, this is not how we win." And interestingly, worked out for you guys. (00:41:19): I want to come back to the brand stuff, but one of the most interesting ways you guys grew early on was influencer marketing, which a lot of people hear about and talk about. I haven't heard much of how to actually do this and what actually works. Talk about that as a broad growth lever for you guys. And then I want to get into just what tools did you use, who actually was really helpful there, thing like that. So yeah, just give us the big picture.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你做了这么多“这不会成”的事。在演示文稿赛道里创业、在扩张中途做整个 rebrand、还有发布后重做整个产品、重新想一切。所有这些，每个人都总说“不，这不是我们赢的方式”。有意思的是，对你们成了。(00:41:19)：我想回到品牌那块，但你们早期发展最有意思的方式之一就是 influencer 营销，很多人听说过、聊过，但我很少听到具体怎么做、什么真的管用。把它作为你们一个大的增长杠杆讲讲。然后我想深入聊你们用了什么工具、谁在那儿真的帮了忙，之类。所以，给我们个大图。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. I think a lot of founders assume that with influencer marketing it's almost like turnkey. You set aside a budget, you find some creators, you figure out the right campaign or the right moment of time to do it and it's all done, you're ready to go. And I think the reality is, going back to this founder-led marketing mindset is like, well, you're going to set yourself up for success if you actually are super involved in that entire process. So for us, what this meant was all the initial influencers I onboarded manually myself. I would jump on a call with each one of them so that they understood what Gamma represented, how to use the product. You want to be able to have them tell your story but in their voice, right? And they can't do that if you're not willing to put in that investment. (00:42:32): And so we would spend a lot of time going through ... It wasn't my job to tell them how to pitch Gamma, but it was my job to make sure that they understood what Gamma was as a product. And so we'd spend a lot of time, like me just walking through the product, them asking questions, us just kind of brainstorming what could the hooks be, and me just giving them some initial feedback and saying, "Oh yeah, this one, I love that. I figure it's going to work great for your audience." But not trying to be super prescriptive. And working with a ton of micro influencers, people that don't have massive followings but are committed to ... Going back to giving value to your audience. They're committed to giving value to their audiences. They want to be able to showcase tools that actually they would use or they are using. And how do you do that in an authentic way? You can't really fake that. You really need to spend the time doing that. (00:43:16): And just like you would onboard a customer, you onboard an influencer the same way. You want them to be an extension of your team. And I think they can feel whether or not you're willing to put in the work. And if you're not, then they're just going to treat it like any other project, ship it and be done with it. If you invest in that relationship, guess what? They'll be back to actually post about you again. And you're all of a sudden having this sort of this relationship that actually you can build over time. I think that's really where the magic is. Too many people discount that initial piece.
turns.zh: 好。我觉得很多创始人以为 influencer 营销几乎是“开箱即用”（turnkey）。你拨一笔预算，找几个创作者，想好对的 campaign 或对的时间点，就全搞定了，可以走了。而现实是，回到创始人主导营销的 mindset：如果你真的全程深度参与，你是在为自己铺成功路。所以对我们来说，这意味着最初所有的 influencer 都是我亲自一个个手动邀请的。我会和每一个人开线上会议，让他们理解 Gamma 代表什么、怎么用这个产品。你要让他们用自己的声音讲你的故事，对吧？如果你不愿投入那个投资，他们做不到。(00:42:32)：所以我们会花很多时间过……我的工作不是告诉他们怎么推销 Gamma，而是确保他们理解 Gamma 作为产品是什么。所以我们花很多时间，我带他们走一遍产品，他们问问题，我们就是一起头脑风暴钩子可能是什么，我给点初始反馈说“噢对，这个我喜欢，我觉得对你受众会很管用”。但不试图太规定死。和大量 micro influencer 合作，那些没有海量粉丝、但很投入的人——回到“给受众提供价值”。他们致力于给受众提供价值。他们想展示自己真的会用、或正在用的工具。你怎么以真实的方式做这个？你没法假装。你真的需要花时间做这个。(00:43:16)：就像你会 onboard 一个客户，你用同样方式 onboard 一个 influencer。你想让他们成为你团队的延伸。我觉得他们能感觉到你愿不愿意投入那个功夫。如果你不愿，他们就只会把它当又一个项目，发完拉倒。如果你投入这段关系，猜怎么着？他们会回来真的再发关于你的内容。你就突然有了这段可以随时间建立的关系。我觉得那才是魔法所在。太多人低估了那最初的一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. To be clear, influencer marketing, essentially a person with a following on say TikTok, Instagram, Twitter, LinkedIn, whatever, gets paid in some way to promote your product. That's the simple way to understand influencer marketing, yeah?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。说清楚，influencer 营销，本质上就是某个在 TikTok、Instagram、Twitter、LinkedIn 之类有粉丝的人，以某种方式被付费来推广你的产品。这是理解 influencer 营销最简单的方式，对吧？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yes, that's definitely the simple way. And I'd say there's definitely different levels. I think a lot of people think influencer marketing and they'll think these big trendy creators, people that have a million followers for instance. And the idea is that, okay, we're going to carve out a really big budget, we're going to choose five or six that we feel like are really the tastemakers in the space and put all of our money into just having them talk about our product. And I think usually this is kind of the wrong approach. Because many of them, they do have massive audiences. And for you, you basically give them a script to read and it immediately feels like an ad. That product is not connected really to them in any way. It's just something that they're ... For this week they happen to be working with you and then they move on with their life. And it never feels organic or authentic and you wasted a ton of money doing so. (00:44:55): I think you're much better doing the hard thing, which is hard to scale, but it's finding the thousands of micro influencers that have an audience where your product maybe is actually useful. And for instance, for us early on it'd be educators, people that for them, part of their job is creating slides every day because they need to engage their students. And so for them, having a tool that actually saved them a ton of time was something they love talking about. And if you can find some of these pockets, we call them echo chambers, where if you find a pocket like educators, teachers love telling other teachers about products they love using. During summer break, they all come together and talk about, "Okay, what are the things that are going to actually improve my job next school season?" And obviously during this AI wave, a lot of those have been, "Okay, what are the AI tools that just save me a ton of time?" (00:45:43): And so if you can start actually tapping into these pockets of echo chambers, that's even better. It doesn't have to be this flashy, well-known influencer. It's actually just this person that has an audience where people really trust what they say. And that's amazing. That ends up becoming this sort of wildfire that can spread really, really fast.
turns.zh: 对，那绝对是最简单的方式。而且我会说确实有不同层次。我觉得很多人一想到 influencer 营销，想到的就是那些很火的、有一百万粉丝的大创作者。思路是，好，我们拨一大笔预算，选五六个我们觉得真是领域里潮流引领者的人，把钱全砸进去让他们讲我们产品。我觉得这通常是错误的做法。因为很多人虽然受众巨大，但对你来说，你基本就是给他们一个剧本照着念，马上就让人感觉像广告。那个产品跟他们之间其实没有任何关联。他们这周碰巧在跟你合作，然后继续过他们的生活。它永远不感觉有机或真实，你还浪费了一大笔钱。(00:44:55)：我觉得你更好的做法是去啃那块难啃但难以规模化的骨头：去找成千上万个 micro influencer，他们的受众群体里，你的产品可能是真的有用。比如我们早期就是教育工作者——对他们来说，工作的一部分就是每天做幻灯片，因为他们要吸引学生。所以对能帮他们省大量时间的工具，他们爱讲。如果你能找到这些“小圈子”（我们叫 echo chambers，回音室），就更好了。比如找到教育者这个小圈子，老师爱跟其他老师讲自己爱用的产品。暑假里他们聚在一起聊：“好，下个学期什么能真的改善我的工作？”显然在这波 AI 浪潮里，很多是“好，什么 AI 工具能帮我省大量时间？”(00:45:43)：所以如果你能开始切入这些回音室小圈子，那就更好了。它不需要是那种高调、有名的 influencer。它其实就是这样一个有受众、人们真信任他说话的人。那很赞。那最终会变成一场野火，扩散得特别特别快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what's the dollar amount these folks get? It's like a few hundred bucks, a few thousand bucks, something like that?
turns.zh: 这些人拿多少钱？几百块、几千块那种？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, few hundred to low thousands, low single digit thousands.
turns.zh: 对，几百到低位几千，个位数的几千。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you find these folks? Is there tools that you use? Is it just like a bunch of manual searching and looking?
turns.zh: 你怎么找到这些人的？有用工具吗？还是就是一堆手动搜索、翻找？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, in the very beginning it was all manual, a lot of cold outreach. And then we ended up finding a couple of different things. One is a platform, a YC company called 1stCollab. That has been amazing. They basically do all of the automated outbound for you. Plus you can help them actually create profiles or personas of different creators, so for instance educators being one, and then they'll go out and actually, based on that profile, find all the right creators for you. So they've been amazing, really great to work with. (00:46:46): And then we've also found small agencies to also help kind of augment that. I look for agencies that are super young and hungry. These are people that they're native to social media and so they really understand it. And they can really be able to bring in creators that are great to work with. And I think part of it is if you find creators that are great to work with, everything else becomes easy. So we've had a few, one is AKG Media, actually out in the UK, and they've been fantastic to work with as well. So you kind of find a few different things, either agencies or platforms that can help you actually scale this thing up.
turns.zh: 对，最开始全是手动，大量冷 outreach。然后我们找到了几样不同的东西。一个是平台，一家 YC 公司叫 1stCollab。超棒。他们基本帮你做所有自动化的对外触达。而且你能帮他们真正建立不同创作者的档案或画像（persona），比如教育者是一个，然后他们会根据那个画像出去真的为你找对所有创作者。所以他们很棒，合作体验很好。(00:46:46)：然后我们也找了小代理公司来补充。我找那些特别年轻、特别饥渴的代理。这些人本身就是社交媒体的原住民，所以真懂。他们能带来很好合作的创作者。我觉得一部分是，如果你找到好合作的创作者，其他一切都容易。所以我们有几个，一个是 AKG Media，在英国，合作也非常好。所以你会找到几样不同的东西，要么代理公司要么平台，能帮你真的把这个规模做起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when they post, they're generally transparent about this is a paid promotion, right?
turns.zh: 他们发的时候，一般会对“这是付费推广”透明吧？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're not just pretending, "I found this tool and I love it"? Cool.
turns.zh: 他们不是假装“我发现了这工具、我好爱它”？酷。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, exactly right.
turns.zh: 对，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And so how much impact did this lever of influencer marketing have on your growth, say from 10 to 100? Is this the biggest lever of growth other than just word-of-mouth, people continue to share it?
turns.zh: 好。那这个 influencer 营销杠杆对你们增长的影响有多大，比如从 1000 万到 1 亿？除了口碑、人们继续分享，这是最大的增长杠杆吗？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, so word-of-mouth has definitely been the biggest. So we look at all new subscriber growth, over 50% of this is word-of-mouth. It's either people searching direct, coming direct, entering Gamma.op, or going through search and typing in Gamma, like a branded keyword search, where they're looking for Gamma, they've heard about Gamma. But I think for us, social media and influencers specifically has always been an amplifier. So every time we invest in influencer marketing, we actually see word-of-mouth increase even more. And it's always like you can just see it. Basically anytime you spend a little bit of money, you start seeing people come through influencer, the word-of-mouth factor actually will get another 1.5 additional users on top of that, which has been really interesting to see. (00:48:29): And I think part of this is just recognizing that ... And I think we kind of understand it, but with influencer marketing, why it's so effective, we all know Dunbar's number, which is have this number of 150 people that you call kind of your network. And your network you trust more than the average stranger down the street. If they tell you something, they recommend something, there is a sort of halo effect, you learn to trust them. A lot of these influencers, the reason why they share so much about their lives is because they want to be in your network. They want you to feel super close. And once you feel super close, you trust them to actually share things that are going to be useful. (00:49:05): And so when they recommend a tool, there is a sort of halo effect, where it doesn't feel like it's coming from a stranger, it feels like it's coming from a friend. And that's where every time we've spent money there you actually see this amplifications, like, "Okay, that's kind of interesting." You wouldn't necessarily expect that. But for us it's been this sort of amplifier from the very beginning.
turns.zh: 对，口碑绝对是最大的。我们看所有的新订阅增长，超过 50% 是口碑。要么是直接搜、直接进来、输 Gamma.op，要么走搜索打 Gamma 这个品牌词——他们在找 Gamma，他们听说了 Gamma。但我觉得对我们来说，社交媒体、尤其是 influencer，一直是放大器。所以每次我们投 influencer 营销，我们其实看到口碑涨得更多。而且总是你能直接看到。基本上你每次花一点钱，你开始看到有人通过 influencer 进来，口碑因素实际上会在那之上再多带来 1.5 个用户，这真的很有意思。(00:48:29)：我觉得一部分只是认识到……我觉得我们算理解，但 influencer 营销为什么这么有效：我们都知道 Dunbar 数（Dunbar's number），就是那种你称之为自己网络的 150 人。你的网络，你比信任街上 average 陌生人更信任。如果他们告诉你什么、推荐什么，会有种光环效应（halo effect），你学会信任他们。很多这些 influencer 之所以分享这么多生活，是因为他们想进你的网络。他们想让你感觉超近。一旦你感觉超近，你就信任他们去分享真正有用的东西。(00:49:05)：所以当他们推荐一个工具，有种光环效应，它不感觉来自陌生人，而像来自朋友。这就是为什么每次我们在那花钱，你真的看到这种放大——“噢，这有点意思”。你不一定预期到。但对我们来说，它从一开始就是这种放大器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so fun to hear about. I've not heard this level of detail on how influencer marketing works and how to make it work. A few more questions here. So you said there's maybe a few thousand people you ended up working with, roughly, influencers?
turns.zh: 听这个太有意思了。我从没听过这么细的 influencer 营销怎么运作、怎么让它奏效。再问几个。你说你们最后大概合作了几千人，influencer，大致？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Over the course of a year. It wasn't all in the same time. Basically in the beginning you do ... In the very, very beginning we had a small budget. It was like 20 creators a month. And then you start increasing that to like 50, then 100. We're definitely not fully scaled at this point, but I could easily see a point where you're working with many, many creators every single month. And that gives you a chance to actually test a variety of, again, content hooks, ways to talk about the product, value props.
turns.zh: 一年下来。不是同一时间。基本上最开始你做……非常非常开始我们预算小，大概一个月 20 个创作者。然后你提到 50，然后 100。我们肯定还没完全铺开，但我很容易想象一个节点——你每月和非常多非常多创作者合作。那给你机会真的测试各种内容钩子、讲产品的方式、价值主张（value props）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And you said the key here is you spend time with every one of these creators, influencers early on to help make sure they understand what you're doing and get excited about it. It isn't just like a thing you outsource.
turns.zh: 厉害。你说这里的关键是，早期你花时间和每一个创作者、influencer 在一起，确保他们理解你在做什么、并对它兴奋。这不是你外包掉的事。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I think there's a lot of value there. It's again hard to quantify. And most founders probably feel like they're too busy to allocate that time. But I think it was a good investment. Because going back to you want them to feel like an extension of your team. They're not going to feel like an extension of your team if, one, they've never met you, and two, you've never even told them really how the product works. They're forced to go to your website to figure it all out. Those are going to be not a whole lot of love that they're feeling from the outset.
turns.zh: 我觉得那里很有价值。再说一遍，难量化。大多数创始人可能觉得太忙，分不出那个时间。但我觉得是好的投资。因为回到你想让他们感觉像你团队的延伸。如果他们从没见过你、从没听你真正讲过产品怎么用，他们被迫去你网站自己搞清楚——那一开始他们就不会有多少“爱”的感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is quality over quantity, especially when you're getting started. And then there's this other piece of niche which I think is very counterintuitive. Instead of going to large influencers with a huge audience, it's good with folks that are small. What's like a audience size roughly that you think is ideal for this, or what niche just means?
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是质量重于数量，尤其起步时。还有另一块“小众”（niche），我觉得非常反直觉。不是去找大受众的大 influencer，而是和小的好。你觉得理想的受众规模大概多大，或者“小众”到底指什么？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Honestly, I don't think there's a minimum, because even with platforms like TikTok, they oftentimes are giving you credit for a brand new account. They want to help amplify that new account, because obviously if they're thinking from a creator perspective, if that new creator feels like, "Oh, coming to TikTok is a massive win for me," they're going to be more invested in it. And so there really isn't a minimum. A lot of these platforms are trying to shift to kind of the same thing, where they really reward new creators on the platform. And so you could have a small audience, it doesn't really matter. You could have 10,000 followers, that's also good. I think as long as the content feels, again, engaging, authentic to the people you're talking to I think it has a really good chance of actually taking off.
turns.zh: 老实说，我觉得没有下限，因为就算 TikTok 这样的平台，他们常常会给一个新账号信用/权重。他们想帮放大那个新账号，因为显然如果从创作者角度想，如果那个新创作者觉得“噢，来 TikTok 对我是个大赢”，他们会更投入。所以真没下限。很多平台都在往同一方向转，真的奖励平台上的新创作者。所以你可以受众小，没所谓。你可以有一万粉丝，也挺好。我觉得只要内容感觉——再说一遍——对你聊的人有吸引力、真实，它就很有机会真的起飞。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point with TikTok, where it's not follower related, if it's useful and people find it clickable or whatever, likable, viewable, the algorithm will spread it to a lot of people. Such a good point.
turns.zh: 关于 TikTok 这点太好了——它跟粉丝无关，如果有用、人们觉得可点击、可赞、可看，算法就会把它推给很多人。太好的点。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's a couple more points you made in the tweet that I want to make sure we highlight. So one is you made this point that 90% of your reach in influencer marketing comes from less than 10% of people. Is there anything there that you think is important for people to hear?
turns.zh: 好，你在推文里还提了几个点，我想确保我们highlight到。一是你说 influencer 营销里 90% 的触达来自不到 10% 的人。这方面有没有什么重要的想让大家听到的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean this just goes back to it's hard to know where that 10% is going to come from. So you kind of just have to cast a super wide net. You can sort of, I think try to, again, trick yourself into thinking you're great at picking creators or you're great at telling them how to post about your stuff. But the reality is, even for me, I could never guess. I kind of had some idea, but I just had to make sure that I was meeting enough creators broadly such that when you meet enough, they're all posting, there's some pocket that end up just taking off. And I was not a good predictor of that. I was not smart enough to actually know which ones would take off. I just knew that we had to play the sort of numbers game to make it work.
turns.zh: 有。这其实就是回到“你很难知道那 10% 会从哪来”。所以你几乎得撒一张超级大的网。我觉得你可能会骗自己相信你很会挑创作者、或很会告诉他们怎么发关于你的东西。但现实是，连我都不可能猜中。我有点想法，但我就是得确保我足够广地接触足够多创作者，这样当你接触够多，他们都在发，总有些小圈子最后就起飞了。而我不是个好预测者。我没聪明到真知道哪些会起飞。我只是知道我们得玩那种数字游戏（numbers game）才能让它成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one of your tips here is people fail often in this because they start too small or their budget's a little too small. You recommend 10,000 to 20,000 a month over six months and just trying this. It sounds like you're doing like 20 to 30 creators a month. Is that the right framework for how to just start this thing and explore?
turns.zh: 所以你这里的一个建议是，人们常失败是因为起步太小或预算有点太小。你建议一个月 1 万到 2 万、持续六个月去试。听起来你是在做一个月 20 到 30 个创作者。这是开始探索这事的正确框架吗？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, totally. And I'd say it's not just that the budget's too small, it would be that they put all their eggs in one basket. So you can also easily blow that 20 K on just one bigger influencer and then be like, "Oh, that didn't work, so I'm going to try it again. That didn't work. Okay, I give up." And I think rather than doing that, you should be like, "Okay, that 20 K, I could actually probably work with 40 different influencers and see what actually works." And across the 40, I'm going to try to find a variety of personas, a variety of use cases, spend a lot of time with them, and then actually see what's working, what's not. (00:53:39): And then next month take those learnings and double down. If educators are working, go with educators. If consultants are working, go with consultants, find more consultants, there's going to be more there. I think that's where the putting all your eggs in one basket is just probably the surest way to fail, because you're going to miss a ton and it's going to take you way too long to learn and you're going to come to the conclusion that it's a waste of time.
turns.zh: 对，完全。而且我会说，不只是预算太小，而是他们把所有鸡蛋放一个篮子里。所以你也很容易把那 2 万全砸在一个大 influencer 上，然后“噢，没用，我再试一次。还是没用。好，我放弃了。”我觉得与其那样，你应该想“好，那 2 万，我其实大概能跟 40 个不同 influencer 合作，看什么真的管用。”在这 40 个里，我试图找各种画像（persona）、各种使用场景，花很多时间跟他们在一起，然后真的看什么管用、什么不。(00:53:39)：然后下个月拿这些 learnings 加倍下注。如果教育者管用，就做教育者。如果顾问管用，就做顾问，找更多顾问，那里会有更多。我觉得把所有鸡蛋放一个篮子，几乎是最确定的失败方式，因为你会错过一大堆，而且得花太长时间学，最后得出“这是浪费时间”的结论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like this whole podcast conversation could be just about this one lever. So much I want to keep talking about, but there's more questions here because this is so useful and interesting. You had this line in your tweet about how reality is not an accident and that this approach is how you figure out what actually works. And then once you do that, then you start leading into that messaging. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 我觉得整场对话都可以只聊这一个杠杆。有太多我想继续聊，但这里还有更多问题，因为这太有用太有意思了。你推文里有一句“现实不是偶然”（reality is not an accident），这种方式是你搞清楚什么真管用的方法。然后你一旦做到，就开始leading into那个 messaging。讲讲这个。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: This goes back to obviously if you're testing a bunch, you'll finally find that sort of post or set of posts that actually go viral. Going back to just the fundamentals, like make it easy for your influencers to be able to tell your story in their voice. One thing we did, we open sourced basically our entire brand. We have Brand.gamma.app, which is everything about our brand, our voice and tone, our art direction, what we use in mid-journey to create the sort of art direction that we have so that a creator can do the same, right? And they can actually just copy all of that so that they don't have to reinvent the wheel every time they're trying to post about Gamma. They have all of that. (00:54:56): And I think going back to this notion of just make it dead simple for them, remove friction. They already have enough on their plate to have to figure out. Don't make it any harder than it is. And if you remove friction, then it's like, oh, you get into this rhythm of adding creators is easy, having them post is easy, reviewing what's working, what's not is easy. And if you're able to do that relentlessly over many, many months, then all of a sudden hitting the sort of viral post is easy because you're going to have enough bats there where some are actually going to pop off. But you only can get there after you've done all the hard work before that to remove friction from the process. And feeling like it's almost like a well-oiled machine at that point.
turns.zh: 这回到显然如果你在测一堆，你终会找到那条、或那组真的病毒式传播的帖子。回到基本面：让你的 influencer 容易用他们自己的声音讲你的故事。我们做的一件事，是我们基本把整个品牌开源了。我们有 Brand.gamma.app，里面是我们品牌的一切——声音语调、艺术方向、我们在 mid-journey 里怎么造出那个艺术方向——这样创作者能做同样的事，对吧？他们能直接复制所有这些，不用每次发 Gamma 都重新发明轮子。他们有全部那些。(00:54:56)：回到那个“让它对他们简单到极致、消除摩擦”的概念。他们盘子里已经够多了，要自己去搞。别让它比本来更难。如果你消除摩擦，那就像——噢，你进入节奏：加创作者容易、让他们发容易、review 什么管用什么不也容易。如果你能连续好几个月无情地做这个，那突然击中病毒帖就容易了，因为你有足够多的“球棒”（bats）在那里，有些会真的爆。但你只有先做足前面那些消除摩擦的苦工才能到那。到那点时感觉像个上油的机器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a platform you find most helpful for the stuff you guys are doing? Is it like TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn, something else?
turns.zh: 你们做的这些事，有没有哪个平台你觉得最有用？是 TikTok、Instagram、LinkedIn，还是别的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean this is one where for us we cast a pretty wide net too. But it's very clear, LinkedIn, the conversion rates are just substantially higher. They're 4X, maybe 5X higher than other platforms. And I think a lot of people are probably still sleeping on LinkedIn, frankly. And so it's one where some of the influencers there or creators there can be a little bit more costly. But if you can eventually be more targeted knowing that, hey, this type of creator is pretty impactful for our product, then working with them, it's just like, "Oh, that's great." The conversion rates are just so strong and it really feels like we're just getting started there. (00:56:22): So if in the beginning you're not sure, it's always helpful to cast a pretty wide net. And then similar to just the influencer strategy, like test and iterate, you'll figure out ... Many of these things will follow a power law. So it's like one or two channels are going to be the most important for you. For instance, Twitter for us hasn't been that impactful. And I think for tools like Notion, they've been really, really impactful. You're not going to really know, and so just test and then double down on the ones that really move the needle for your product.
turns.zh: 有。这方面我们也撒了挺广的网。但很明显，LinkedIn 的转化率就是高得多。是其他平台的 4 倍、可能 5 倍。而且老实说，很多人可能还在忽视 LinkedIn。所以那里一些 influencer 或创作者可能贵一点。但如果你最终能更精准地知道“嘿，这类创作者对我们产品挺有冲击力”，那跟他们合作就“噢，太好了”。转化率就是强，而且感觉我们才刚起步。(00:56:22)：所以如果你一开始不确定，撒广网总是有用。然后类似 influencer 策略——测试、迭代，你会搞清楚……很多这种事会遵循幂律（power law）。所以会是一两个渠道对你最重要。比如 Twitter 对我们一直没那么大冲击。而对 Notion 那种工具，Twitter 就真非常非常有冲击。你不会真的知道，所以就是测试，然后加倍下注在那些真能推动你产品指针的渠道上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that many people listening now are like, "Wait, LinkedIn posts are sponsored sometimes? I didn't know that." How do you know if it's a sponsored post? Is it like a #sponsored or something like that? How do they communicate this?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多听的人现在在想“等等，LinkedIn 帖子有时是赞助的？我不知道啊。”你怎么知道它是赞助帖？是那种 #sponsored 之类的吗？他们怎么传达这个？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Usually they'll say they're a partner or yeah, basically it is sponsored in some form, or they'll #ad or something along those lines. So that's probably the way you'll see it the most.
turns.zh: 通常他们会说自己是个 partner，或者基本就是某种形式的 sponsored，或者他们发 #ad 之类的。所以那大概是你最常看到的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. By the way, I don't do this sort of stuff. Have you ever seen me on LinkedIn? I'm not doing any paid stuff. It's just so people know. And I don't plan to do that. (00:57:19): This episode is brought to you by Miro. Every day, new headlines are scaring us about all the ways that AI is coming for our jobs, creating a lot of anxiety and fear. But a recent survey for Miro tells a different story. 76% of people believe that AI can benefit their role, but over 50% of people struggle to know when to use it. Enter Miro's Innovation Workspace, an intelligent platform that brings people and AI together in a shared space to get great work done. Miro has been empowering teams to transform bold ideas into the next big thing for over a decade. Today, they're at the forefront of bringing products to market even faster by unleashing the combined power of AI and human potential. Guests of this podcast often share Miro templates. I use it all the time to brainstorm ideas with my team-
turns.zh: 酷。顺便说，我不做这种事。你在 LinkedIn 上见过我做这种吗？我没做任何付费的。就是让大家知道。而且我不打算做。(00:57:19)：本期由 Miro 赞助。每天，新标题都在吓我们——AI 以各种方式来抢我们工作，制造大量焦虑和恐惧。但 Miro 最近一项调查讲了不同的故事。76% 的人相信 AI 能惠及他们的角色，但超过 50% 的人不知道什么时候该用它。于是有了 Miro 的 Innovation Workspace，一个智能平台，把人和 AI 聚在一个共享空间里完成出色工作。十多年来，Miro 一直赋能团队把大胆想法变成下一个大东西。今天，他们通过释放 AI 和人类潜力的合力，站在更快把产品推向市场的最前沿。本播客嘉宾常分享 Miro 模板。我总用它和团队头脑风暴——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Often share Miro templates. I use it all the time to brainstorm ideas with my team. Teams especially can work with Miro AI to turn unstructured data, like sticky notes or screenshots, into usable diagrams, product briefs, data tables, and prototypes in minutes. You don't have to be an AI master or to toggle yet another tool. The work you're already doing in Miro's Canvas is the prompt. Help your teams get great work done with Miro. Check it out at miro.com/Lenny. That's M-I-R-O .com/Lenny. Let's come back to this brand point. So, one of your big lessons is invest in brand before you go heavy into hit paid ads and performance marketing. I imagine you do some ads at this point on Facebook and Google and things like that.
turns.zh: ……常分享 Miro 模板。我总用它和团队头脑风暴想法。团队尤其可以用 Miro AI 把非结构化数据，比如便利贴或截图，在几分钟内变成可用的图表、产品简介、数据表和原型。你不必是个 AI 大师，也不必再去切另一个工具。你在 Miro Canvas 上已经在做的工作，就是 prompt。帮你的团队用 Miro 完成出色工作。去 miro.com/Lenny 看看。那是 M-I-R-O .com/Lenny。我们回到品牌这个点。所以你一个大教训是：在重金砸付费广告和效果营销之前，先投资品牌。我猜你们这阶段在 Facebook、Google 之类上做了些广告。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, we run ads performance marketing. I think there's this stigma that brand marketing and performance marketing are sort of at odds with each other. I very much follow the sort of thought that brand marketing is performance marketing. Everything is some form of performance marketing. It just might not be as attributable, so the ability to actually map back to every single dollar spent is a little bit harder, but it doesn't mean that it's not impactful. (00:59:12): And I think as a company scales, you have to invest in both, and ideally they work really, really well together. The more you invest in brand marketing, it strengthens your performance marketing. This goes back to having enough creative to even test. If you're too limited in scope and you don't have a brand, you feel like you can actually amplify your handicapping, your ability to actually have a good performance marketing program.
turns.zh: 对，我们跑效果营销广告。我觉得有种成见，认为品牌营销和效果营销是彼此对立的。我非常认同“品牌营销就是效果营销”这个思路。一切都是某种形式的效果营销。只是它可能没那么好归因，所以把每一块钱花出去映射回去的能力难一点，但不代表它没冲击。(00:59:12)：而且我觉得公司扩展时，两者都得投，理想是它们配合得非常好。你在品牌营销上投得越多，它强化你的效果营销。这回到“有足够创意去测”。如果你范围太窄、没有品牌，你会感觉自己在削弱——削弱你真正搞好一个效果营销项目的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that heuristic of how do you know if you are under invested in brand is if you're limited in the number of ideas you can try in performance marketing.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个启发法（heuristic）：你怎么知道自己品牌投资不足？就是看你在效果营销里能试的想法数量是不是受限了。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is your design system just... Is everyone having to redesign things from scratch and come up with all these frameworks every time they run an ad?
turns.zh: 你的设计系统就是……每个人每次跑广告都得从零重设计、想出所有这些框架吗？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah, yeah. Basically you kind of have a feeling for, "If I were to scale this up to a thousand pieces of creative, would it still feel cohesive or is it kind of all over the place?" And if it feels like it's all over the place, then you kind of have to go back to the drawing board.
turns.zh: 对，正是。基本你会有种感觉：“如果我把这个扩到一千个创意，它还会感觉统一吗，还是乱七八糟？”如果感觉乱七八糟，那你得回画板。

turns.speaker: Lenny
