turns.en: You said when you talked about the rebrand, that it took a lot longer than you expected, that it was more expensive than you expected. That's the fear, I think, everyone has when they hear this like, "Oh, I don't have time for a rebrand." I also imagine, because your product is so visual, that it makes more sense to invest there and to spend the time and money. (01:00:23): For the typical founder, do you have any just, I don't know, thoughts of just like, "Here's when it makes sense. Here's a sign you really need to invest here heavily." Versus, "It'll probably be all right."
turns.zh: 你说 rebrand 时，它比你预期久得多、比你预期贵得多。我觉得那是每个人听到“噢，我没时间做 rebrand”时的恐惧。我也猜，因为你们产品这么视觉化，在那投资、花时间花钱更说得通。(01:00:23)：对典型创始人，你有没有什么想法，比如“这里是什么时候说得通、什么信号说明你真得重金投这里”，相对“大概还行”?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I do think it's probably more geared toward anything that's a little bit more prosumer or consumer because so much of your product, you're trying to create this feeling for a user, what are they experiencing. And the experience happens way before they even drop into your product. It might be they see an ad or they see a billboard or they see something. It's like, "Okay, that piqued my interest a little bit." (01:00:56): And then you need some sort of symmetric messaging in that they see there's some symmetry in that, they see the ad, then they drop into the product or they land on your website, it feels cohesive and it feels like, "Okay, this is interesting. I'm going to go all the way through to sign up and then maybe actually start using the product." (01:01:12): That's a little bit different when it's a B2B product or where there isn't as much reliance on that initial moment. They might just hear about it through a colleague and then sign up for it and then go through a huge procurement process and then it's like, "Okay, maybe it matters, but probably not so much as for a product where the brand can have so many different touch points."
turns.zh: 有。我觉得它可能更偏向任何稍微 prosumer 或 consumer 的东西，因为你产品很大一部分是在给用户创造一种感觉——他们在体验什么。而那个体验发生在他们甚至还没进你产品之前。可能是他们看到广告、看到广告牌、看到什么。像“噢，那稍微勾起我兴趣了”。(01:00:56)：然后你需要某种对称的 messaging——他们看到广告和进产品/落地页之间有对称性，感觉统一，像“噢，这有意思。我要一路走到注册，然后也许真的开始用产品”。(01:01:12)：那对 B2B 产品或没那么依赖那个初始瞬间的，有点不同。他们可能就听同事说起，然后注册，然后走个大采购流程，然后“好，也许重要，但对一个品牌能有这么多触点的产品来说，大概没那么重要”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about some broader things that have worked to help you grow, but before we do that, I just want to visualize the pie chart of how Gamma grows. Say, post-10 million ARR. If I have it correctly in my head, it's over 50% just word of mouth, organic, people are sharing it, doing presentations for each other, "Oh, it's Gamma. Just go check it out, sign up." Then it feels like the second-biggest bucket is influencer marketing, social stuff. And then is the third performance/paid marketing?
turns.zh: 我想聊些帮助你们增长的更广泛的事，但在此之前，我想可视化一下 Gamma 增长的饼图。比如 1000 万 ARR 之后。如果我脑子里对的话，超过 50% 就是口碑、自然、人们互相分享、给对方做演示——“噢，是 Gamma，去看看、注册”。然后第二大块是 influencer 营销、社交类。第三是效果/付费营销？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yep, that's right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. On that last piece, is there anything else there for people that are starting to explore performance marketing, essentially Facebook Ads, Google Ads, all these other platforms, is there anything else that you think might be helpful for people to hear or learn just to get started down this road?
turns.zh: 酷。最后那块，对开始探索效果营销、基本就是 Facebook Ads、Google Ads、所有那些平台的人，还有没有什么别的你觉得有用、该让人听到或学到的，来起步走这条路？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I would just have two recommendations. One, going back to my initial piece of advice, which is don't invest until you have word of mouth. Don't fool yourself into thinking that you'll solve other problems by just starting to ramp up a performance marketing program. Just get the word of mouthpiece first, so that you're coming into this program with some tailwinds and then start ramping it up. (01:02:40): The second piece is: set some constraints. You don't want your product to be at a point where more than 50% of your acquisitions are coming through paid acquisition. I think if that is happening, your core growth engine is broken. And it feeds right back to point number one, which is if your core growth engine is broken, you just have this leaky bucket. You're trying to spend so much money building top of the funnel, people are not making it all the way through. Something else should be fixed before you really try to dial it up. And it doesn't mean you don't spend a little bit of money, but just don't dial it up until you feel like your core growth engine is actually working.
turns.zh: 我就两个建议。一，回到我最开始的建议：在你有口碑之前别投。别骗自己以为靠启动一个效果营销项目就能解决别的问题。先把口碑那块拿到，这样你进这个项目时有些顺风，然后再开始加码。(01:02:40)：第二点是：设些约束。你不想让你的产品到一个点——超过 50% 的获客来自付费获客。如果那发生了，你的核心增长引擎是坏的。它直接回到第一点：如果核心增长引擎坏了，你就是个漏桶。你花那么多钱建漏斗顶部，人却走不到底。在真加码之前，别的什么该先修好。不代表你一分钱不花，但在你感觉核心增长引擎真在运作前，别加码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you said the first point about wait until you have word of mouth before investing in performance marketing, is that essentially a large chunk of your growth should be coming from word of mouth, direct, organic?
turns.zh: 你说第一点“等有了口碑再投效果营销”，本质是你们增长的一大块该来自口碑、直接、自然？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And for us, even at scale, again going back to more than 50% of new signups still come through word of mouth. That, for us, is a sign like, "Okay, if something is still working, people are using the product, telling other people, then you want that feeling before you really start dialing anything else up."
turns.zh: 对对。对我们来说，就算在规模上，回到“超过 50% 的新注册还是来自口碑”。对我们来说，那是个信号：“好，如果有什么还在起作用、人们用产品、告诉别人，那你想要那种感觉，再真去加码别的任何事”。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a percentage that you think is helpful for people to think about just... Is it 25% or more something like that or just word of mouth for you to feel like, "Okay, we actually have organic growth as a major growth engine"?
turns.zh: 有没有个百分比，你觉得有助于人们去想——是 25% 或更多、还是只要口碑让你觉得“好，我们真把自然增长当主要增长引擎了”？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I think this comes back to maybe just how maybe aggressive you want to be. I think just rough heuristic is the more, the better. If it's over 50%, I think that's great. If it's approaching that, good. And just going back to, don't fool yourself into thinking just ads is going to be the way you grow. Because you can do that, but everything else becomes harder and harder. (01:04:16): If you rely on paid acquisition to be the main growth engine, you should be prepared for things like CAC, like customer acquisition costs, to keep going up. The more you're trying to reach a new audience, it gets more and more expensive. So, don't assume it's going to be flat, and then all of a sudden you're running on this treadmill that's actually running faster and faster. And so that's where it's easy to get hooked on that early on when you're just investing a small amount of money, and then it's almost impossible to get off that treadmill when you're too far into it. So, anticipate that and give yourself a better chance at actually being able to sustain that growth long-term.
turns.zh: 有。我觉得这回到你有多激进。粗略启发法就是越多越好。如果超过 50%，我觉得超棒。如果接近那个，也好。回到别骗自己以为光靠广告就是你的增长方式。因为你能那么做，但其他一切会越来越难。(01:04:16)：如果你依赖付费获客做主要增长引擎，你该准备好 CAC（客户获取成本）之类一直往上走。你越想触达新受众，越贵。所以别假设它会平，然后突然你跑在一台越来越快的跑步机上。所以早期你只投一点钱时很容易上钩，等你陷太深就几乎下不了那台跑步机。所以预期到这个，给自己更好机会真正长期维持那个增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Important advice. Okay. There's a couple more elements you've shared that were key to Gamma's growth. One is sharing prototypes with users before you ship. What does that look like? What does that mean? Why is that so powerful?
turns.zh: 重要的建议。好。你还分享了几样对 Gamma 增长关键的元素。一个是“在 ship 之前和用户分享原型”。那长什么样？什么意思？为什么那么强？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, this for us was a huge unlock. Going back to early days, when you're just trying to get your product into anybody's hands, you're getting to your friends trying to use it, and again, they're going to lie to you, tell you how great it is, and then never come back to using the product. (01:05:19): I think what you want to be able to do, the ideal situation is, you recruit a bunch of people that are legitimately good prospective users or customers of your product, but have zero skin in the game. They do not care at all whether or not your product succeeds. They're just in it to test it. And for us, it was people that have made slide decks or make slide decks regularly, let's drop them into Gamma, give them very little context. We just tell you, "Hey, this is an alternative to PowerPoint. Go ahead and try it." (01:05:48): And then as you're going through the onboarding flow and testing the product, just tell us everything that's going on in your head, describe what you're seeing, tell us what you're trying to do. We'll give you maybe a few different tasks like, "Oh, create a piece of content." And when you watch them do that and also hear what they're saying, you just immediately feel the pain. (01:06:10): All the places they're struggling and all the places are so confused by what they're seeing and you sort of then can internalize that pain and say, "Okay, we're going back and we have to fix this. This is not usable." We, oftentimes, are dog-fooding everything. And so you can get to the point where you're so familiar with your own product, everything feels kind of easy and you know where things are, but when you start actually hearing other people describe their usage of the product, that's a gift. (01:06:36): You're all of a sudden you're like, "Okay, now I know where to actually spend the time." People aren't even getting to the third screen. They're stuck on the first screen because they can't even find the button that we think is so dead obvious, and so let's go back and actually re-engineer, re-architect that piece of it. (01:06:50): And we've done that for everything: landing pages, onboarding experience, new feature launches, export, sharing, every single piece of that such that we can actually see where things are working or not. And then every time, we'll learn something that's kind of painful, but obvious that we need to fix and we go back and fix it.
turns.zh: 有。对我们来说这是个巨大的解锁。回到早期，你只想把产品塞进任何人手里，找朋友试，再说一遍，他们会骗你、告诉你多棒，然后永不回来用。(01:05:19)：我觉得你想做的、理想情况是：你招募一批真的是优质潜在用户或客户、但和这事毫无利益关系的人。他们完全不在乎你产品成不成功。他们就是来测的。对我们来说，是那些做过、或定期做幻灯片的人，把他们放进 Gamma，给极少背景。我们就告诉你：“嘿，这是 PowerPoint 的替代品。去试吧。”(01:05:48)：然后当你走引导流程、测产品时，把你脑子里一切告诉我们，描述你看到的，告诉我们你想做什么。我们可能给你几个不同任务，比如“噢，造点内容”。当你看着他们做、也听到他们说的，你立刻感到那个痛点。(01:06:10)：他们卡住的所有地方、被看到的的东西搞糊涂的所有地方——你就能内化那个痛，说“好，我们回去得修这个。这没法用”。我们常常对所有东西做 dog-fooding（吃自己的狗粮）。所以你会到一种程度——你对自己产品太熟，一切感觉容易、你知道东西在哪，但当你真开始听别人描述他们怎么用产品，那是个礼物。(01:06:36)：你突然“好，现在我知道时间该花哪了”。人们甚至到不了第三个屏。他们卡在第一屏，因为连我们认为超明显的按钮都找不到，所以回去真正重新设计、重新架构那块。(01:06:50)：我们对每样东西都这么做：落地页、引导体验、新功能发布、导出、分享，每一块都这样，这样我们真能看到哪在起作用、哪没。然后每次我们都学到点痛但明显、需要修的东西，回去修掉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you scale this sort of thing? How do you run every new big idea, new feature change by people? Do you have a closed beta group, a decent platform? How do you actually do this?
turns.zh: 你怎么扩展这种事？你怎么让每个新大想法、新功能改动都过一遍人？你有个封闭 beta 组、不错的平台？你具体怎么做这个？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: There's a couple of great platforms. Voicepanel, which is also YC company, full disclosure, angel investor, and then there's also platforms like UserTesting, that really help you source and find these people that fit again, that persona or profile you're looking for. So, in our case, people that are in a specific job function or create decks regularly, and so you can use those platforms to really scale up these programs pretty fast. (01:07:45): And then once your team knows how to use those platforms... We would have an idea in the morning and in the afternoon, we're already running a pretty full scale experiment or a research study, and by the evening or by the next day, we can actually go through all of it together. So, it's pretty fast once you have it set up. It's more about how do you get the program onboarded the right way. (01:08:06): I think the other sort of mechanism we did early on was once we had some repeat users, we created sort of a program for our power users. We called it the Gammaster Program, which is we put them into a separate Slack workspace, and that was a place for us to share very, very early prototypes like wireframes, sometimes they were functional prototypes, and get them to get some initial feedback as well. This definitely helps with more later stage or features or things that aren't going to be necessarily important as part of onboarding, but once you understand Gamma, like, "Oh, how do you share it?" (01:08:41): For instance, this was a great way to start testing some of that because they already understand Gamma, but now you're adding that new functionality. And then we can also watch them struggle and hear how they're struggling with the product. And so that has been a great way just to have a separate Slack workspace. Anytime we're thinking about something, they're the first to hear about it. Give us some early indication if we're on the right track or not.
turns.zh: 有几个很棒的平台。Voicepanel，也是 YC 公司，坦白说我是天使投资人，还有像 UserTesting 这样的平台，真的能帮你 sourcing 并找到符合那个画像或画像的人。所以对我们来说，就是那些在特定职能上、或定期做 deck 的人，你可以用那些平台很快把这类项目规模做大。(01:07:45)：一旦你团队知道怎么用那些平台……我们早上有个想法，下午就已经在跑相当大规模的实验或研究，到傍晚或第二天我们就能一起过完所有内容。所以一旦设好就挺快。更多是“你怎么把项目以对的方式 onboard”。(01:08:06)：我觉得早期我们做的另一种机制是：一旦有了一些回头用户，我们为 power users 做了个项目，叫 Gammaster Program（Gamma 大师计划）。我们把他们放进一个独立的 Slack workspace，那是我们分享非常早期原型——比如线框图，有时是能用的原型——并拿到一些初始反馈的地方。这肯定有助于更后期阶段的、或不一定作为引导重要、但一旦你理解了 Gamma 的功能，比如“噢，你怎么分享它？”(01:08:41)：比如，这是开始测其中一些的好方式，因为他们已经理解 Gamma，但现在你在加那个新功能。然后我们也能看着他们卡住、听到他们怎么跟产品挣扎。所以有个独立 Slack workspace 是个好方式。任何时候我们在想什么，他们第一个听到。给我们早期信号，看我们走没走对路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this workflow that you shared of you have an idea in the morning, you built a prototype. Do you built it with AI prototyping tools like Cursor, Lovable, something like that?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你分享的这个工作流：早上有个想法，你做了个原型。你是用 AI 原型工具做的吗，比如 Cursor、Lovable 之类的？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yep. That or it could be... Yeah, I mean we're lucky a lot of our designers also know how to code, so even before the recent tools, come up with some sort of functional prototype and then be able to ship that so people can start playing with it.
turns.zh: 对。或者可能……对，我是说我们幸运的是很多设计师也会写代码，所以即使在最近这些工具出现之前，也能做出某种能用的原型，然后能 ship 出去让人开始玩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, you have an idea in the morning, you build a prototype using various tools. By the end of the day, you are getting feedback from real people using one of these platforms, Voicepanel or UserTesting, and just that loop saves you, I imagine, potentially months of just building the thing nobody wants and shipping it, launching it, and then just failing.
turns.zh: 对。所以你早上有个想法，用各种工具做个原型。到一天结束，你就通过 Voicepanel 或 UserTesting 这类平台从真实用户那拿到反馈，光是这个循环，我猜就帮你省了——可能几个月的、去建一个没人要的东西、发布它、然后失败。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah. I think this is even more probably helpful for certainly a lot of folks that are starting to do much with vibe-coded apps. Yeah, that's great. You've lowered the amount of time to get something out there. Now, prove that it's useful to some set of users, and this should be again, every day, every week, you should be able to go through a ton of these, and then build on the things that seem to be working. (01:10:08): I feel like that's almost like a way to speed run a lot of that early... you're in the idea maze, you think you have something that could kind of work. How do you actually break through so that people are actually finding value in what you're building?
turns.zh: 完全对。对。我觉得这对很多开始大量做 vibe-coded（氛围编程）应用的人，可能更有帮助。对，你降低了把东西弄出去的时间。现在去证明它对某群用户有用，而且这应该again，每天、每周，你都应该能过一大堆这种，然后在那些似乎管用的东西上继续建。(01:10:08)：我觉得那几乎像加速跑通很多早期……你在想法迷宫里，你觉得有点东西可能管用。你怎么真的突破，让人们真的在你建的东西里找到价值？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love it because so many people hear this idea of just run your stuff by users before you do the user research. It sounds so hard and heavy lift-y, and the way you're describing it is very automated, very quick to do. You don't have to go think about finding random people in a coffee shop. It's just like these platforms exist where you could go plug in your thing, get feedback by the end of the day.
turns.zh: 对，我喜欢，因为太多人听到“在做事前先拿给用户跑一遍”这个想法。听起来好难、好重。而你描述的方式是非常自动化、非常快就能做。你不用去想“在咖啡店找随机的人”。就是这些平台存在，你插进你的东西，一天结束就拿反馈。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah, and that helps you just move way faster.
turns.zh: 完全对。对，那帮你快非常多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a feature that you were super excited about that you built and ran through this and just like, "Okay, that was a huge failure"?
turns.zh: 有没有哪个功能你超级兴奋、建了、跑过这个流程，然后就“好吧，那是巨大的失败”?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I don't think any of the ones where we... We always try to chunk it down. So, none of the things we're testing earlier on are these massive features. They're always an inception or a starting point of, "This could be something interesting." (01:11:07): And then we take that initial learning and actually then build the product around it. It's never like, "Oh, we spent four months working on this thing. Let's see if anybody actually wants it." It's almost like we always start super early. And then a bunch of ideas die right away, but they're still pretty small ideas. (01:11:20): And then the ones that kind of pass the initial test, you start building towards something that could be, hopefully, more game-changing or much more value-add. And by the time you're actually shipping, you've gone through 10 different layers of actually testing and iteration before it actually sees the light of day.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们测的都没有……我们总是试图把它切成小块。所以早期测的都不是这些大功能。它们总是一个起点或开端——“这可能有点意思”。(01:11:07)：然后我们拿那个初始学习，真的围绕它建产品。从来不是“噢，我们花四个月搞这东西。看有没有人要”。几乎总是我们超早开始。然后一堆想法立刻死掉，但它们还是挺小的想法。(01:11:20)：然后那些过了初始测试的，你开始朝可能有更大改变、或更大价值的方向建。等你真 ship 时，它已经过了 10 层不同的测试和迭代才见光。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really interesting about you and the way your company operates, you guys are ex-Optimizely people, so you're very versed in experimentation. A lot of people talk about A/B testing experimentation as something that doesn't make sense for a startup because the scale is so low. What I'm hearing here, and I know this is something you talk about, is just there is actually a lot of ways to think experimentally, even in the early stages. Is there something more there you think is important for people to hear?
turns.zh: 你和你们公司的运作方式真正有意思的是，你们是 ex-Optimizely（前 Optimizely）的人，所以你们非常熟 experimentation。很多人说 A/B 测试实验对初创公司没意义，因为规模太小。我这里听到、而且我知道这是你聊的，是其实有很多方式可以抱着实验的心态去思考，哪怕在早期阶段。还有没有什么更重要的想让人听到？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah. I really think it's more of... The mindset you go into to almost any problem or opportunity is the saying of, "Strong opinions weakly held." I think it's totally fine to have some of these assumptions or hypotheses going into a lot of these things, but you should always know that there's a way to start trying to validate some of this. (01:12:20): As a founder, you're always trying to build conviction, and so you build conviction by not having it all live in your head, but getting it out there and start testing this with users, prospect customers, and starting to see what are the things that actually feel right. And sometimes you have enough data to be statistically significant. Sometimes it's more of a, "Hey, we at least were able to gut check this a little bit and get some qualitative feedback." I think that's still valuable. It shouldn't be this sort of all or nothing like, "It has to be static for it to be useful." I don't think that's true. (01:12:49): In fact, I'll just share the very early story of when we first started Gamma, we knew we wanted to help change the way people communicate, and we actually had two different ideas we were parallel pathing kind of at the same time. Of course we had presentations, reimagining how people were creating presentations, and we also actually had this separate idea, which we called The Lobby, which is a virtual office. This is a place where this is, again, peak pandemic, much more hybrid work, much more virtual work. And so this was a place where everybody on the team, whether you're in the same office or not, could gather, collaborate to feel pretty magical. (01:13:26): And we worked on both for six months. We worked on both the virtual office and the presentation product for six months. We would dog-food both. So, oftentimes we'd be in the virtual office, presenting the presentation tool and kind of use both. And after six months, we came to this conclusion that we wanted to go all in on the presentation tool. And the reason was, when we looked at the virtual office tool, we were sort of always competing against what we thought was something we'd never be able to surpass, which is in real life experience, actually being able to work shoulder to shoulder with your colleagues and having this environment where you really feel like you're building together. (01:14:05): Virtual office could get pretty good, but we would never beat that. And so we were almost limited in our own imagination about how good could this product be versus the presentation product. We ended up with a million more ideas we thought we could actually introduce that could be better than how you work in PowerPoint today. We were just so energized by it. (01:14:25): And so for us, that was this sort of A/B test of testing these two things that we invested equal amount of time into, and coming out at the other end realizing that, one, was going to be the product we were pour all of our blood, sweat and tears into making it great because we saw the potential in it.
turns.zh: 有。我真的觉得更多是……你带着去面对几乎任何问题或机会的 mindset，是那句话“强观点、弱持有”（strong opinions weakly held）。我觉得带着一些假设或假设去搞这些事完全没问题，但你总该知道有办法开始验证其中一些。(01:12:20)：作为创始人，你总在试图建立 conviction（信念），而你建立 conviction 不是让它全活在脑子里，而是把它弄出来、开始和用户、潜在客户测试，开始看哪些东西真的感觉对。有时你有足够数据到统计显著。有时更多是“嘿，我们至少能稍微 gut check 一下、拿到一些定性反馈”。我觉得那也有价值。不该是“要么全有要么全无，必须统计显著才有用”那种。我觉得那不对。(01:12:49)：其实，我分享个很早的故事：我们刚起步 Gamma 时，我们知道想帮人改变沟通方式，而且我们其实同时在并行两条想法。当然我们有演示文稿——重新构想人们怎么做演示；我们还有个独立想法叫 The Lobby（大厅），是个虚拟办公室。这是 peak pandemic 时，更多混合办公、更多虚拟办公。那是个地方，不管你在不在同一办公室，大家都能聚在一起、协作，感觉挺魔法。(01:13:26)：我们两个都搞了六个月。虚拟办公室和演示产品都搞了六个月。我们都 dog-food 两边。所以常常我们在虚拟办公室里，演示演示工具，两个都用。六个月后，我们得出结论：要 all in 演示工具。原因是，看虚拟办公室工具时，我们总在跟一个我们觉得永远超不过的东西竞争——就是真实生活体验，能跟同事肩并肩工作、有那种真在一起建东西的环境。(01:14:05)：虚拟办公室能做得挺好，但我们永远打不赢那个。所以我们在自己想象力上受限——这产品能多好，相对演示产品。我们最后有上百万个想法，觉得真能引入、比你现在用 PowerPoint 的方式更好。我们超级受鼓舞。(01:14:25)：所以对我们来说，那就是对这两样东西的 A/B 测试——我们投了等量时间，到最后意识到其中一个，会是我们倾注所有心血去做到极致的产品，因为我们看到了它的潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that about you guys, that you explored that other idea. There's so many startups that did that during COVID times, and like, "Okay, this is the future. We're all going to be remote, and let's work remotely in virtual offices." There's a startup and I'm a tiny investor in, Lindy, that is now a big AI agent company, and they did the same thing. I imagine that was their whole first concept. It was just these little avatars. It was like a little game where you walk around, go to little virtual meeting rooms.
turns.zh: 我不知道你们还探索过那个想法。COVID 时有太多创业公司那么做，像“好，这是未来。我们都要远程，在虚拟办公室里远程工作”。有家创业公司，我是个小投资人，Lindy，现在是个大 AI agent 公司，他们也这么干过。我猜那就是他们整个最初概念。就是这些小头像。像个你走来走去、进小虚拟会议室的小游戏。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, it was a fun product to work on, but yeah.
turns.zh: 对，那是好玩的产品，不过对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting how we just reverted back to the mean of just like, "Yeah, people are in offices again. That was a fun experience." Although things have changed. Just to highlight this point you made that I think is really powerful, I haven't heard it described this way before, just the power of testing prototypes very, very, very early, using these platforms that make it super easy. (01:15:34): We always hear, "Okay, you have a mock, you have a prototype. Yeah, testing with users always feels like this heavy thing. You got to have a user research team, go do interviews, do one-on-ones." What you're describing is something... I don't know why everyone's not doing this. With AI tools, it's so easy now. Have an idea, build the prototype, test it with, I don't know, is it like dozens of people? How many people actually run through a prototype on average?
turns.zh: 对，有意思的是我们怎么就回到了均值——“对，人们又回办公室了。那是段好玩的经历。”虽然事情变了。就 highlight 你这点，我觉得很有力，我从没听过这么描述过——就是极早期测原型的力量，用这些让这事超容易的平台。(01:15:34)：我们总听到“好，你有个 mock、有个原型。对，跟用户测总觉得是很重的事。你得有个用户研究团队，去做访谈、做一对一。”你描述的……我不知道为什么大家不都这么做。有 AI 工具，现在超容易。有个想法，建原型，测——我不知道，是几十个人吗？平均一个原型实际有多少人看过？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 20 people. So, 20 people look at this thing, give you a bunch of feedback, you realize this was very dumb, or, "Here's the nugget that we want to lean into." And instead of building a thing, instead of doing all these user research sessions, things like that. Super cool. (01:16:12): Okay. Is there any other big lesson or lever that has helped you grow to today's 100 million ARR, and $2 billion company? We talked about influencer marketing, we talked about testing prototypes, investing in brand and a little bit of paid growth. Anything else?
turns.zh: 20 个人。所以 20 个人看这东西，给你一堆反馈，你意识到这超蠢，或者“这是我们要深挖的那个 nugget（内核）”。而不是去建个东西，而不是做所有这些用户研究环节之类。超酷。(01:16:12)：好。还有没有别的大教训或杠杆，帮你们增长到今天 1 亿 ARR、20 亿估值的公司？我们聊了 influencer 营销、测原型、投资品牌、一点付费增长。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Certainly for us, the ability to adapt and move fast in this environment. I attribute a lot of what we've been able to accomplish to a few things. One is we do have a small team and a lean team, one that's able to move really fast. I think that means, by default, we have to look for a lot of levers where a small team can do a lot of different things. (01:16:54): So, we can talk, one, obviously about how do you construct a team like ours and what I think has worked. And then two, going back to experimentation being this sort of thing where for us it's been a huge unlock because it allows you to not only test things and iterate a ton, it allows you to build much more efficiently. And so we've been in a startup where we've had great unit economics from the very beginning. We run profitably, we have really strong margins. (01:17:22): I don't think that would be possible if experimentation wasn't core infrastructure to us because the temptation would be you just throw the most expensive model at every job and assume that's going to work. And the reality is that never is the case. And so for us to be able to actually test across 20 different models in production today, always trying to align the kind of value we're delivering to our customers with our ability to actually scale this operation, that's been in the background. (01:17:48): And not always things that are easily quantifiable or things that you're sharing broadly, but it is core to our DNA. And again, going back to a team that came from Optimizely, probably not surprising, but I do think that's been part of our ability to actually execute at this level.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，当然是能在这环境里适应、快速行动的能力。我把我们能取得的很多成就归因于几件事。一是我们确实有个小团队、精益团队，能超快行动。我觉得那意味着，默认情况下，我们得找很多杠杆，让小团队能做很多不同的事。(01:16:54)：所以，一，显然可以聊怎么构建像我们这样的团队、什么管用。二，回到 experimenting 这件事——对我们来说它是个大解锁，因为它不仅让你测东西、大量迭代，还让你更高效地建。所以我们这家创业公司从一开始就有很好的单位经济效益（unit economics）。我们盈利地跑，毛利很强。(01:17:22)：我觉得如果 experimenting 不是我们的核心基础设施，那不可能，因为诱惑会是你把最贵的模型砸到每个任务上、假设那会管用。而现实从不是那样。所以对我们来说，今天能在生产环境里跨 20 个不同模型测，总是试图把我们交付的价值、和我们能真正规模化的运营能力对齐，那一直在背后。(01:17:48)：而且不总是容易量化、或你广泛分享的东西，但它是我们 DNA 的核心。再说一次，回到来自 Optimizely 的团队，可能不意外，但我确实觉得那是我们能在这个水平执行的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that the product is so beautiful and such a good experience. It's such a good example of experimentation and being really obsessed with running experiments, A/B tests. Data can create really beautiful products and experiences that aren't just feeling like some kind of micro-optimized flow.
turns.zh: 我喜欢产品这么美、体验这么好。它是 experimentation、真的痴迷跑实验、A/B 测试的好例子。数据能造出真正美的产品与体验，而不只是感觉像某种微优化流程。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah. And just going back to one part of the team, part of that plays a huge role, which is you want to build a product where people talk about taste and brand and all these things, what they emote. I'm not going to throw in whether or not, yes or no, but I do think it makes a difference. And for us, at some point, more than a quarter of a team or about a quarter of our team was product designers. I think that's an unintuitive level of investment, or at least that's not common. You don't see many startups at our stage or early stage where a quarter of the team's product designers. (01:18:55): And I think that was an important investment for us because when you think about with AI companies, so many companies are trying to invent new surface areas or new user experiences, and that's not possible if you're not really getting the foundation right, really thinking deeply about user problems and how can you solve them in a novel way. And so for us, we made that investment in the very beginning, even if it was counter to what other startups would do, because we actually felt like it was the right thing.
turns.zh: 完全对。对。回到团队那部分，其中有巨大作用的是——你想建一个人们聊品味、品牌、所有这些他们情绪化的东西的产品。我不会硬说行或不行，但我确实觉得那有区别。对我们来说，有段时间超过四分之一、或大概四分之一的团队是产品设计师。我觉得那是个反直觉的投资水平，或至少不常见。你在我们这个阶段或早期，看不到很多创业公司有四分之一团队是产品设计师。(01:18:55)：我觉得那对我们是重要的投资，因为想 AI 公司时，那么多公司在试图发明新界面或新用户体验，而如果你不把基础做对、不深想用户问题、怎么用新颖方式解，那不可能。所以对我们来说，我们从最开始就做了那个投资，哪怕它跟别的创业公司相反，因为我们真觉得那是对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I definitely want to spend more time on hiring. Before we get to that, you've touched on this kind of concept that you guys are, what many described, a GPT wrapper company. You essentially sit on top of other models, do some cool stuff, charge for that. There's historically, and there's been a big shift here, historically, there's this sense that, "Okay, you're just this thin layer on top of the model. How is there any sort of motor leverage or long-term business model here when it's just the model that is doing the thing and charging you guys to do all this AI work?" (01:19:57): It feels like people have started to realize maybe that is the only place money will be made because the models are just so hard to compete with, and that's not a place you can build a business anymore. Talk about just what you've learned about this concept of being a GPT wrapper, and what people may not be understanding about the business opportunity there.
turns.zh: 好。我肯定想多花时间在招聘上。在到那之前，你提到了你们被很多人描述为“GPT wrapper 公司”。你基本是架在其他模型之上，做些酷的东西，据此收费。历史上——而且这里有大转变——历史上人们觉得“好，你只是模型之上薄薄的一层。当只是模型在做这事、还收你们钱做这些 AI 工作，这里哪有什么护城河或长期商业模式？”(01:19:57)：现在感觉人们开始意识到，也许那才是唯一能赚钱的地方，因为模型太难竞争了，那不再是你能建生意的地方。聊聊你对“做 GPT wrapper”这个概念学到了什么，以及人们可能没理解那里的商业机会。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: When you think about maybe just literally only being a wrapper on one model or one provider, yeah, maybe there's only limited amount of utility or value add. But then when you start thinking about, "Okay, I'm going to go really deep into this one workflow, and it's not just one model." It's maybe 20 plus models powering all different parts of the product, and then you're thinking about the orchestration that's required and you're thinking about, obviously if you're experimenting constantly being able to test across the newest models versus models that have been around that are cheaper, you're doing a lot to really... Your job is to, again, align value, maximize the value you're delivering to the end user in a way that's sustainable for you as a business. And so there's a lot more to that. (01:21:00): And so for us, we've always been passionate about being very close to our customers, our users. Who, for them, their job to be done is visual communication, visual storytelling. And the default tool today is going into a PowerPoint or Google Slides where the amount of effort to create something... We've all been there late at night trying to format a deck, trying to find the right layout, all this manual and tedious work. (01:21:24): Well, what if you could abstract all that away and give them something that feels a little bit more delightful, a little bit easier, much more effortless? What would that earn you in terms of a customer that wants to come back to your product? And so that's everything that we focus on is you need to go deep into the workflow, be empathetic to the user and their job that you're trying to solve, and of course, apply the best technology possible so that you're delivering on that promise of a product experience that's way better than the status quo. (01:21:52): And I think if you can be laser-focused on, it doesn't matter if you're a wrapper or not, what is the technology you're doing and applying, that makes a real difference? So, that's the ultimate goal.
turns.zh: 当你想的可能只是字面意义上一个模型、一个提供方之上的 wrapper，对，也许只有有限效用或价值增量。但当你开始想“好，我要在这个工作流里钻很深，而且不只是一个模型”。可能是 20 多个模型在驱动产品的各个不同部分，然后你想的是所需的编排（orchestration），你想的是——显然如果你不断实验、能跨最新模型和更便宜的老模型测，你做了很多去……你的工作，再说一遍，是对齐价值，最大化你交付给终端用户的价值，同时对你作为企业可持续。所以那里多得多。(01:21:00)：对我们来说，我们一直热衷于离客户、用户很近。对他们来说，他们的待办工作是视觉沟通、视觉叙事。而今天的默认工具是进 PowerPoint 或 Google Slides，那里要付出大量努力才能做出东西……我们都经历过深夜试图调格式、找对的排版，所有手动又繁琐的活。(01:21:24)：那如果我能把那些全抽象掉，给他们点感觉更愉悦、更容易、更不费力的东西呢？那会为你赢得一个想回来用你产品的客户多少？所以我们聚焦的一切就是：你得钻进工作流、对用户和他们要解的问题有共情，当然还要用最好的技术，去兑现“产品体验远好于现状”的承诺。(01:21:52)：我觉得如果你能激光聚焦——不管你是不是 wrapper，你在做、在用的技术，真有区别吗？所以那才是终极目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a really cool framework for how to think about what it takes to build a successful wrapper company that is... I don't know, I'll keep using that term. I don't know if it's [inaudible 01:22:09], but just some ideas don't work. These model companies are launching their own products here and there. (01:22:16): So, what I love about what you're describing here is almost like a heuristic that'll tell you if there's an opportunity/how to be successful as a GPT "wrapper company." I'm putting in air quotes. It sounded like maybe there's three here. But talk about just if you think about the bullet points of what you need to do to build a successful business on top of existing models.
turns.zh: 这是个超酷的框架，讲怎么想“建一家成功的 wrapper 公司”需要什么——我不知道，我继续用那个词。我不知道这是否[听不清 01:22:09]，但有些想法就是不行。这些模型公司在这那发布他们自己的产品。(01:22:16)：所以我喜欢你描述的，几乎像个启发法，能告诉你有没有机会、怎么作为 GPT“wrapper 公司”成功。我加了空气引号。听起来可能有三个点。但聊聊，如果你要想“在现有模型之上建成功生意”需要做的要点。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I mean, I think the most important thing is before we even talk about the technology, so we're skipping to the part where you're trying to apply the most interesting models or technology to solve some problem. Start with solving the problem you actually care about. (01:22:53): I think it's very tempting right now to chase shiny objects, like a founder might be able to gain some initial traction by literally being that GPT wrapper and solving any sort of problem. And you start to see some traction and then you just go with that. But before you do that, you should think about, "Is this a problem I can invest five to 10 years into actually solving? Do I care deeply enough about it?" (01:23:13): Because if you can't, you're never going to go... actually think about overcoming the variety of different hurdles, whether it's other startups or other incumbent tools that are trying to start doing the same thing. (01:23:24): And so for us, we go back to... We've started this company because we really care about helping change the way people communicate their ideas. We really feel like this idea of visual communication, visual storytelling matters. It helps elevate everybody and it gives people much more opportunity to do the things that in the past if you weren't great at making slides, your ideas might've died, and someone else that was able to actually articulate their ideas better ended up winning the deal or winning the favor of their manager or their boss. (01:23:53): And so we felt like that was the wrong, that didn't feel right, and so could we help democratize visual storytelling, visual communication? That was sort of our north star. And then you go back into thinking, "Okay, every step of the way, what are the tools and technology I can apply to help solve that and actually move the average person closer to that long-term vision of ours?" (01:24:14): And of course, AI has been, again, this gift where yes, you can apply that to solving this job. You can also apply that AI to many different jobs. Figure out what is the problem you care deeply enough to go deep, because going back to this sort of idea, you need to own the sort of end-to-end workflow. A customer needs to have... You want your product to live in their brain somewhere where when they think about, "Hey, I have to create a presentation." They come to you as the default tool. (01:24:40): And the moment they start creating it to the moment they ship it and send it to their boss, that end-to-end experience needs to feel magical, needs to feel great. And I don't think you can really do that unless it's actually a workflow you either know deeply yourself or you care deeply to actually help solve for somebody else.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得最重要的是，在我们甚至聊技术之前——我们跳到了你试图用最有趣的模型或技术解某个问题的部分。先从解你真在乎的问题开始。(01:22:53)：我觉得现在很有诱惑去追 shiny object（闪亮物件），比如创始人可能靠字面意义上当那个 GPT wrapper、解任何问题获得一些初始牵引。你开始看到牵引，然后就顺着走。但之前你该想“这是我能投五到十年真去解的问题吗？我够在乎它吗？”(01:23:13)：因为如果你不能，你永远走不到……真去想克服各种障碍，不管是别的创业公司还是别的老牌工具在试图做同样的事。(01:23:24)：对我们来说，我们回到……我们创这家公司是因为真在乎帮人改变沟通想法的方式。我们真觉得视觉沟通、视觉叙事重要。它提升每个人，给人们在过去更多机会——如果你不擅长做幻灯片，你的想法可能就死了，而另一个更能表达想法的人最后赢了这个单、或赢得经理老板的青睐。(01:23:53)：所以我们觉得那不对，那感觉不对，所以我们能帮视觉叙事、视觉沟通民主化吗？那是我们的北极星。然后你回过头想“好，每一步，我能用什么工具和技术帮解那个、真把普通人朝我们长期愿景推近？”(01:24:14)：当然，AI 又是那份礼物——对，你能用它解这待办工作。你也能用它解很多别的待办工作。搞清楚什么是你够在乎、能钻深的问题，因为回到这个点，你需要拥有那种端到端工作流。客户需要……你想让你的产品住在他们脑子某处——当他们想“嘿，我得做个演示”，他们默认来找你。(01:24:40)：从他们开始建、到 ship、发给老板，那端到端体验必须感觉像魔法、必须很棒。我觉得除非那真是个你要么自己深懂、要么够在乎真帮别人解的工作流，否则你做不到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, some of the elements I'm hearing here is, one, is just like actually really care about solving this problem, not come from, "Oh wow, this cool thing happened and it worked. Wow, maybe I could sell this thing to people." Because you may end up having to work on this thing for 10, 20 years.
turns.zh: 所以我这里听到的一些元素：一是真的够在乎解这问题，不是来自“噢哇，这酷东西发生了、管用了。哇，也许我能把这东西卖给别人”。因为你最后可能得在这东西上干 10 年、20 年。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two is: understand the problem really, really deeply and have real empathy for the people trying to solve this problem. You have this problem creating presentations at your previous job, so you understood it, and I imagine you understand even more deeply now that you worked on this. Essentially, care really deeply, go really deep on the problem, have real empathy for the people facing this problem, and then there's this actually be able to solve this problem using the technology out there. (01:25:39): And you made this point about how you guys use 20 different models to do what you do. Talk a little bit more about that just because people may think, "Oh, okay, I could just go to ChatGPT or Claude and it'll create an awesome presentation for me." Why does it take 20 different models? Why is that such a big part of the success here?
turns.zh: 二是：极深地理解问题、对试图解这问题的人有真共情。你之前工作有做演示的这个问题，所以你理解它，我猜你现在做了这之后理解更深。本质上，够在乎、在问题上钻很深、对面对这问题的人有真共情，然后才有“能用现有的技术真解这问题”。(01:25:39)：你说了你们用 20 个不同模型做你们的事。多聊点，因为人们可能想“噢，好，我直接去 ChatGPT 或 Claude，它就能给我做个超棒演示”。为什么要 20 个不同模型？为什么那是成功的一大块？

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, so going back to the workflow, you're trying to go and break down every step of the creation process for a user. So, the moment of the initial idea to maybe creating an outline of what you want to present or articulate to creating the first draft. What do we show you there to editing the content? (01:26:14): Like, "Okay, I have a first draft, but it's only 60% of the way there. How do I get to 100% of the way there?" Those are all things that might require different models. The initial outline might be better served by something that's purposed-built for actually creating the best outline, the best narrative, the best story arc, versus one where you're actually going back and saying... Gamma, our agent can actually go and review your entire deck and say, "Actually, if I were to add suggestions, I would say, 'You may want to change the visual layout on these set of cards, and you may want to actually change the imagery or the visuals for these cards to match everything else.'" (01:26:50): These are things that, again, every model might be better served for different things. And so knowing how that actually breaks down into the end user, sitting down, working on the product, working on their presentation, how do you help them? I think you can only do that by understanding-
turns.zh: 对，回到工作流，你试图分解用户创建过程的每一步。从初始想法，到也许建个你要讲什么的大纲，到建出初稿。我们在那给你看什么、到编辑内容？(01:26:14)：像“好，我有初稿，但只到 60%。我怎么到 100%？”那些可能都需要不同模型。初始大纲可能更适合用一个专为造最好大纲、最好叙事、最好故事弧线而做的东西，相对另一个你回过头说……Gamma 的 agent 能真的去 review 你整个 deck 说“其实，如果我要给建议，我会说‘你可能想改这组卡片的视觉排版，你可能想真改这些卡片的图或视觉，来匹配其他所有东西’”.(01:26:50)：这些事，再说一遍，每个模型可能对不同事更好。所以知道它怎么分解到终端用户——坐下来、用产品、做演示——你怎么帮他们？我觉得你只有理解——

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Their presentation, how do you help them? I think you can only do that by understanding that workflow and then breaking that down into finding the right tool for the right job.
turns.zh: ——他们的演示，你怎么帮他们？我觉得你只有理解那个工作流、然后把它分解、为正确的工作找正确的工具，才能做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super interesting. Essentially there's like, here's the things that AI has to do for us. I don't know, imagining some kind of a storyboard and then it's figure out the model and level of model and prompt for that model to achieve each of these steps as best as possible.
turns.zh: 那超有意思。本质上是有“AI 得为我们做的这些事”。我想象某种 storyboard（故事板），然后为每个步骤算出模型和模型级别、以及那模型的 prompt，尽可能最好地达成。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah, and it applies to even on the visual side, finding the right image. I think certain models are great at photorealistic output versus others want more of the artistic vibe or something that feels more abstract. And so again, you can choose the right model for the right job. It doesn't mean that you'll never use other models, it's just like as you're going through that workflow, the content might dictate what's the best use case. So in that particular use case and so you're always trying to map to that, what is the end user trying to accomplish in that certain moment?
turns.zh: 完全对。对，这也适用于视觉侧——找对的图。我觉得某些模型擅长照片级真实输出，另一些更想要艺术感、或更抽象的感觉。所以again，你能为正确的工作选正确的模型。不代表你永远不用别的模型，只是当你走过那个工作流，内容可能决定什么是最好的用例。所以在那个特定用例里，你总在试图映射到：那个瞬间终端用户想完成什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which models are you finding most useful in the work? I don't know, is there anything surprising about, "Oh wow, this model's actually really good at this and this is really bad at that."
turns.zh: 哪些模型你觉得在工作中最有用？我不知道，有没有什么让人意外的——“噢哇，这个模型其实特擅长这个、这个特不擅长那个”?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I think surprising or not surprising, the leaderboard is constantly changing and so this is where you almost, you have to have the mindset that you can be adaptable. We're just getting to the point where there's going to be more personalization too, is going back to a consultant's going to have different needs than an educator. Educator's trying to engage their students. They may want to have language or visuals are more animated and that makes sense. Consultant can't get away with that. They may need something that is much more structured or information dense. And so again, how do we actually be the same tool that can serve both of those needs? I think that's where it becomes interesting and it's almost like there isn't necessarily even a "best model". It's like what's the right model for that particular user? That's actually a much harder problem to solve and we're just starting to try to embrace some of that now.
turns.zh: 有，我觉得意外或不意外，排行榜一直在变，所以你几乎得有那种能适应的 mindset。我们刚到也有更多个性化的点——回到顾问的需求和教育工作者不同。教育工作者想吸引学生。他们可能想要语言或视觉更生动，那说得通。顾问没法那么搞。他们可能需要更结构化、信息密度更高的东西。所以again，我们怎么真成为同一个能服务这两种需求的工具？我觉得那才是变有意思的地方，而且几乎像没有“最好的模型”。更像是那个特定用户什么模型对？那其实是难得多的问题，我们刚开始试着拥抱其中一些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there one that's just like, "Oh, that's actually really cool." For something that we didn't expect?
turns.zh: 有没有哪个让我们“噢，那其实超酷”，是我们没预期的?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Early on, things like creating the outline, Perplexity was actually great. Not one that people talk about as often, but creating the outline and doing web search and actually integrating some of those elements together for us was pretty powerful.
turns.zh: 早期，像建大纲，Perplexity 其实很棒。不是人们常聊的那个，但建大纲、做 web 搜索、把其中一些元素整合起来，对我们挺强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's two more things I want to talk about. One is pricing. How you guys figured out your approach to pricing. You guys started monetizing really early and that feels like such an important piece to AI startups because you're spending real money on an inference and other things. And then I want to talk about hiring. So in terms of pricing, when did you decide it was time to really start charging and then how did you pick your approach to pricing your actual price?
turns.zh: 好，还有两件想聊的。一是定价。你们怎么想出定价方式的。你们很早就开始变现，那对 AI 创业公司似乎是极重要的一块，因为你在推理（inference）和其他东西上花真金白银。然后我想聊招聘。所以定价方面，你们什么时候决定真开始收费，然后又怎么选你的定价方式和实际价格?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: So we kind of stumbled into having to do pricing and packaging. I mentioned our big AI launch in March 2023. This was pre-revenue, so we wanted just to get, we focused all of our effort on the first 30 seconds, literally all hands on deck, just trying to get that right. And we spent zero time on actually monetization. So we had a credit system. All new users get 400 credits. Once they burn through those credits, there was actually nothing more you could do with AI. It kind of just got cut off. And so Intercom for us was just blowing up with people saying, "How do I purchase more credits? I want to keep using this thing." In a very fair question. So basically all of April we ended up having to do a quick sort of pricing and packaging exercise. We did a couple of different things. (01:30:18): We did run a form of Van Westendorp, which is just understanding-
turns.zh: 我们基本是跌跌撞撞地不得不做定价和打包（packaging）。我说过 2023 年 3 月那次大 AI 发布。那是 pre-revenue（收入前），所以我们只想——我们把所有精力放前 30 秒，全员上阵，就试图把那做对。我们在变现上花了零时间。所以我们有个积分系统。所有新用户得 400 积分。一旦烧完，AI 就啥也做不了了。基本就被切断。于是我们的 Intercom 爆了，人们说“我怎么买更多积分？我想继续用这东西。”很合理的问题。所以基本整个四月我们不得不快速做个定价打包练习。我们做了几样不同的事。(01:30:18)：我们跑了种 Van Westendorp（一种定价调研），就是理解——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Classic.
turns.zh: 经典。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: ...what is the overall willingness to pay. And so we did use that. We did kind of integrate some forms of conjoint analysis, which is just trying to understand what are the features or things that people actually value in your product. And so we'd survey a lot of our early users and ended up coming to a price point that was, in the beginning we only had one plan type. It was roughly like 20 bucks a month. Part of this was also just realizing we almost didn't need to overthink it too much because this is when the initial wave of AI companies and startups were coming out and products are coming out and you almost end up becoming anchored by, what does ChatGPT charge? Because everyone becomes familiar with that price point. And so we ask ourselves how complicated do we want to make it? (01:31:05): We always default to remove friction, make it as easy as possible for a user to understand. And so we end up coming up with a similar price point and ship that as the V1, basically end of May 2023. And for us, we wanted to see a couple of things like, okay, we have the initial price point. Is it economical for us at that price point? Are we actually making money? And we'd monitor there for that for many, many months realizing that yes, actually at that price point we could still generate pretty good margins and that would allow us to reinvest that profit back into growing the business. (01:31:37): Continue to add obviously head count, but then also investing even more into inference costs, whatever we wanted to do to experiment broadly with AI. And so we've always had that pricing and packaging. Does it not only need to be easy to understand for a user, obviously you have to have strong conversion rates, but it should be something where you feel like you could build an enduring durable business off of. And if it's not right, then you can always go back and try to tweak things, but it's something you should be monitoring as early as possible.
turns.zh: ——整体支付意愿（willingness to pay）。所以我们用了那个。我们也整合了些 conjoint analysis（联合分析）的形式，就是试图理解人们实际看重你产品里的哪些功能或东西。所以我们调查了很多早期用户，最后到了一个价格点——一开始我们只有一种套餐类型。大概一个月 20 块。这部分也是意识到我们几乎不需要过度纠结，因为那是第一波 AI 公司和产品出来的时候，你几乎会被锚定在“ChatGPT 收多少？”因为大家都熟悉那个价格点。所以我们问自己：要把它搞多复杂？(01:31:05)：我们默认消除摩擦，让用户尽可能容易理解。所以我们最后搞了个类似的价格点，作为 V1 ship 出去，基本是 2023 年 5 月底。对我们来说，我们想看几件事：好，我们有了初始价格点。在那个点对我们经济吗？我们真在赚钱吗？我们监控了好几个月，意识到对，在那个点我们仍能产生相当好的毛利，那能让我们把利润再投回增长业务。(01:31:37)：当然继续加人头，但也更多投到推理成本、任何我们想广泛实验 AI 的事。所以我们一直有那个定价打包。它不只需要对用户容易理解——显然你得有强转化率——还得是你觉得能建一家持久耐用生意的东西。如果不对，你总能回去调，但那是你该尽早监控的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting, we have the head of ChatGPT on the podcast and he shared the way they picked ChatGPT's prices is the Van Westendorp survey that they ran in Google Forms.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我们请了 ChatGPT 的负责人上播客，他分享他们选 ChatGPT 价格的方式，就是在 Google Forms 里跑的 Van Westendorp 调研。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Yeah, I listened to that one. Yeah, it was a great one.
turns.zh: 完全对。对，那期我听了。对，超棒的一期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, what a, that survey man, what a, and not only just that survey being the slick, I'm imagining that XKCD comic with the open source little, I don't know, block holding up the entire world, like this one little piece of code. That's like the survey, just behind everything. But it's interesting how that one decision just created this ripple effect on all AI startups, 20 bucks a month. Of course that's what everyone's doing.
turns.zh: 噢，那调研，老兄，那调研，而且不只是那调研很顺滑——我在想那个 XKCD 漫画，开源的小方块撑起整个世界，就像那一小段代码。那就像那个调研，躲在一切背后。但有趣的是那一个决定就在所有 AI 创业公司上造了涟漪效应，一个月 20 块。当然大家都在这么做。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Who knows what would happen if they chose a different number, but here we are.
turns.zh: 完全对。谁知道如果他们选了不同数字会怎样，但我们在这了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone would be so much more rich if it's just like 25 bucks. Someone. Imagine the GDP of growth-
turns.zh: 如果就 25 块，大家都会富多啦。有人。想象那带来的 GDP 增长——

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ...from that. Oh man. Okay. And then the way, so was Van Westendorp helped you pick a price point and then you said this conjoint analysis, we actually have a guest post that I think describes how to do this well and if not we'll find, appoint people to how to actually approach this. You started charging, so was post product [inaudible 01:33:11] launch, you launch with no paid features. People were just like, "I want to pay, I want to keep using this." You're like, "Okay, I guess we've got to start charging."
turns.zh: ——从那来的。噢老兄。好。然后方式是，是 Van Westendorp 帮你选了价格点，然后你说的联合分析，我们其实有篇嘉宾帖讲怎么做好这个，如果没有我们会找、指派人讲怎么实际入手。你们开始收费，所以是 Product Hunt[听不清 01:33:11]发布之后，你们发布时没有付费功能。人们就说“我想付钱、我想继续用”。你们就“好，我猜我们得开始收费了”。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: That's right. Yep.
turns.zh: 对。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything, looking back, I guess just you wish you'd known when you were approaching pricing for folks that are doing this now like, "Oh, we should have done this differently or should have thought about this."
turns.zh: 有没有什么，回头看，我猜是你希望对正在做定价的人的建议——“噢，我们应该 differently 做这个、或应该想过这个”。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean that one's hard. I think you never want to obviously just throw something together without giving it much thought, but for us with limited resources, we focused on the only thing we thought mattered, which was getting some initial users and having that organic growth. And I think there's maybe two checkpoints of thinking about whether or not you feel like you have product market fit. I think one checkpoint is organic growth. The second is are people willing to pay for the product? And I think if you pass both those, you feel like you've, at least within some pocket of the market you have some PMF. So I think those are both important questions to ask depending on your resources. Ideally you can do kind of both and experiment a little bit along at the same time. And then by the time you actually have paying users, you sort of check some of those boxes for yourself.
turns.zh: 有，我是说那个难。我觉得你显然永远不想啥都不想就拼凑一个，但对资源有限的我们，我们聚焦在唯一我们认为重要的事——拿到一些初始用户、有自然增长。我觉得关于“你是否觉得有产品市场契合”可能有俩检查点。一个是自然增长。二是人们愿不愿意为产品付钱？我觉得如果你过了这两个，你感觉至少在市场某个小圈子里有了一些 PMF。所以我觉得这两个都是该问的重要问题，取决于你的资源。理想是你能两者都做、同时稍微实验。等你真有付费用户，你就给自己打了些勾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, I love that your launch pricing. You're like, "Okay, let's figure out if we're actually making money or not." It's not obvious with AI companies. [inaudible 01:34:24]
turns.zh: 顺便，我喜欢你们发布定价的方式。你们“好，看我们到底赚不赚钱”。对 AI 公司那不明显。[听不清 01:34:24]

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Well, we also didn't have a choice because at that point runway was also low. So if we weren't making money, well we would actually be in a tough spot.
turns.zh: 对，我们也没选择，因为那时跑道也低。所以如果我们不赚钱，那我们真会很难受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point that you did not have a huge amount of money sitting around to spend on the way a lot of companies in AI do, just, "We'll deal with it and we'll figure out how to make money later."
turns.zh: 这点太好了——你们没有一大笔钱可以像很多 AI 公司那样花在路上一“我们以后处理、以后再想怎么赚钱”。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally. Within a couple of months we had hit a million in ARR and became profitable. And so those were both two exciting milestones for a company that months prior were heads down figuring out how we even survive.
turns.zh: 完全对。几个月内我们就到了 100 万 ARR，并盈利了。所以那两个都是对公司激动的里程碑——几个月前我们还在埋头想怎么活下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a story. I'm so excited to be telling this story. Okay, final topic I want to talk about is hiring. You have some really hot takes on hiring, clearly it's worked out for you guys. What are some things you've learned about hiring well, what is your approach to hiring?
turns.zh: 什么故事。我太兴奋能讲这个故事。好，最后一个话题是招聘。你对招聘有些很辣的观点（hot takes），显然对你们奏效了。你对“招得好”学到了什么，你的招聘方式是什么?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: So we had this mantra internally, I mean even before the sort of AI launch for us, which was "Hire painfully slowly." And I think the temptation is once things start working, you just start, [inaudible 01:35:23] scaling this thing and start adding more and more headcount. And for us that always, I don't know, that didn't feel right. We wanted to build the team very thoughtfully, be lean, but also be a team that every individual feels like they have high amount of impact that they have on a daily basis. And so for us that was from sort of the very beginning. And so even as we've scaled up, I think we've been super efficient by nature of just being a very lean team.
turns.zh: 我们内部有个信条，甚至在那次 AI 发布之前——就是“极其缓慢地招人”（Hire painfully slowly）。我觉得诱惑是，一旦东西开始管用，你就开始[听不清 01:35:23]扩张这事、加越来越多人头。对我们来说那总感觉不对。我们想非常用心地建团队，精益，但同时是个每个人都觉得每天有高影响力的团队。所以对我们那从很早就如此。就算我们扩了，我觉得我们因为精益团队本质而超高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think a lot of people hear this advice of "Stay lean, be efficient." You have some even more concrete pieces of advice here of just what that looks like. You have a huge, I don't know, philosophy of just huge leverage per person. You focus a lot on revenue per employee. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人听到“保持精益、高效”这种建议。你还有些更具体的建议，讲那长什么样。你有个巨大的——我不知——人均高杠杆的哲学。你很聚焦人均营收（revenue per employee）。讲讲那个。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: So obviously we look at things like revenue per employee, but we never let that be the sort of North Star. It's not something that dictates our strategy per se. Same thing with profitability. I think by being efficient, that ends up becoming a side effect of yeah, we are profitable and growing. But I think for us more is like we care a ton about adding the right team members. So it's easy. You can almost sort of shoot yourself in the foot as a founder by just setting the wrong goals. If your goal is to double in headcount and add a hundred people to the company, then that becomes the goal. The goal is no longer to add the best people. It's no longer to maintain a high quality bar. The goal is to hit a hundred people and that's everything everyone's focused on. So then guess what? (01:36:44): If that's the goal, then the thing that ends up dropping is, okay, maybe we will settle for employees that are good enough and we're going to make sure we get to that hundred because a hundred is going to help us get to the next phase of growth. And then the next phase of growth. And I think we've tried to resist that temptation, which is we want everybody that comes through the door and joins our team to really be the type of person that represents Gamma. Our first 10 to 12 employees, we spent so much time really getting the DNA right. I think Brian Chesky talks about this. Your goal is you get that first 10 and you want to be able to then replicate the next 10 and then replicate the next 10, but that 10 needs to be all super cohesive. You need to have the same shared values, same principles, same ambition, same vision, and if you don't, then what are you even replicating? (01:37:32): Right? At that point you're just adding headcount and you can easily just be adding headcount because we're chasing the next shiny startup to join. And so for us, we really focused on that first 10. That allows us to really have this sort of community of teammates that basically want to stick around. A lot of founders think about not wanting to have a leaky bucket on the product side, but the same thing applies on the team side. If you have a leaky bucket, people are just constantly leaving, revolving door. That's a huge amount of cost. The continuity cost is massive and it's really hard to quantify. (01:38:08): And I mentioned our first 10 employees, all 10 of them are still here today, five years later. And so that sort of continuity, it means that you have this tribal knowledge that sticks with you. It means that people can continue building and having that sort of cohesive feeling. So I think that's one piece that's just like, it's hard to quantify, but I do think, new startups I would advise just to really be thoughtful about that, get that to a point where you really feel confident that as you're adding the next 10 and next hundred, you're actually replicating the same DNA and not actually just adding a bunch of random people to the company.
turns.zh: 显然我们看人均营收这类东西，但我们从不让那成为北极星。它不本质决定我们的战略。盈利性也一样。我觉得通过高效，那变成“我们盈利且在增长”的副作用。但对我们更多是我们超在乎加对的团队成员。所以很容易——创始人几乎能通过设置错的目标搬起石头砸自己脚。如果你的目标是人头翻倍、加一百人，那目标就变成那个。目标不再是加最好的人。不再是维持高质量标准。目标是到一百人，那成了所有人聚焦的一切。所以猜怎么着？(01:36:44)：如果那是目标，那掉下去的就是——好，也许我们将就够好的员工，我们要确保到那一百人，因为一百人能帮我们到下一阶段增长。然后下一阶段增长。我觉得我们一直抵抗那诱惑，就是我们想每个进门加入团队的人，真成代表 Gamma 的那种人。我们前 10 到 12 个员工，我们花大量时间真把 DNA 做对。我想 Brian Chesky 聊过这个。你的目标是拿到前 10 个，然后你能复制下 10 个、再复制下 10 个，但那 10 个得全超 cohesive。你得有同样的共享价值观、同样原则、同样野心、同样愿景，如果没有，那你到底在复制什么？(01:37:32)：对吧？那点你只是在加人头，你很容易就加人头，因为我们追着下一个闪亮创业公司去加入。对我们来说，我们真聚焦那前 10 个。那让我们真有这群想留下来的队友。很多创始人想的是产品侧不想有漏桶，但团队侧同理。如果你有漏桶，人不断走、旋转门。那是巨大成本。连续性成本巨大，而且很难量化。(01:38:08)：我说过我们前 10 个员工，10 个今天都还在，五年后。所以那种连续性，意味着你有跟着你的部落知识（tribal knowledge）。意味着人们能继续建、有那种 cohesive 的感觉。所以我觉得那是其中一块——难量化，但我确实觉得，对新创业公司我会建议就是真用心对待那个，到你有信心——加下 10 个、下 100 个时，你是在复制同样的 DNA，而不是真就加一堆随机人进公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of your very specific piece of advice is hire generalists versus someone that's just really deep in one thing, why is that so important? What does that look like?
turns.zh: 你一个很具体的建议是招通才（generalist），相对只在一个事上钻很深的人，为什么那么重要？长什么样?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: This very much feels like the age of the generalist or the rise of the generalist right now. When we think about of a team that can be really flat, you still want people that can be very spiky in certain areas. So for instance, obviously a product designer that knows how to code, that's great. It allows you to actually span across many different domains. And again, an organization that's super flat, when you're wearing a lot of different hats, that means every individual, if you're a generalist, you can wear by default a lot of different hats. And that's helped us just maintain this idea that the work, the opportunity in front of us can easily expand. Each person plays a huge role. They don't need to wait and ask for permission. They can go after and pick up a piece of work because it's there and they can at least get it started even if they're not the one that always sees it through. (01:39:34): And so for us, I do think this rise of the generalist is going to be important. You can always augment that by working with contractors or agencies that are hyper-specialized in certain areas. And this is where, for instance, going back to influencer marketing, you might work with an agency rather than kind of scale up your own influencer marketing team. You work with a hyper-specialized team there. But my marketing team is all generalists. Our head of marketing more recently launched this cool drone show in San Francisco. We have 4,000 people in San Francisco. The mayor came by, she created that entire project and managed that entire project end to end herself while also managing the entire marketing team. And so it's like this idea that a generalist is able to play all these different roles, can still be super high impact. For us, it also goes hand in hand with, I mentioned sort of this other role, which is the player coach. Traditional management layer is like a manager manages a ton of people and that's kind of their core focus. (01:40:33): All of our people leaders are player coaches in that they still do the end work themselves and they can mentor and coach those around them. This analogy came from, or this mindset came from, it's something I borrowed from just the sports world in general because there's a lot of sports that just move incredibly fast. Like football for instance, it moves really, really fast. And so you might have a coach that's calling into play, but the quarterback can actually make a last-minute adjustment based on what he's seeing the defense do. And so you want a player that is on the field that can adapt as needed and that way the coach doesn't have to call every single thing in. He's just kind of giving you the general intent of what you want to run as the play and then the quarterback can still make the adjustments. (01:41:13): And so all of our people leaders, our management layer is all folks that actually can make those adjustments. If they're seeing something that doesn't feel right on a daily or weekly basis, they're adjusting priorities for that team and they're still doing the work themselves too. They're so close to it that they understand what is the relative prioritization at all times. So both of those I think have been, when I think about founders, they oftentimes think about innovation in the sense, we're going to innovate on products or innovate on technology. I think every founder today has a chance to innovate on org design, and that starts by just thinking about what is the type of company we want to build today? What does it mean? And when it comes to the management later, what type of sort of leaders do we hire? What does it mean when it comes to hiring specific roles and specific functions? All of that is a chance for you to be very thoughtful and build a company that you're excited to be at for hopefully many, many years to come.
turns.zh: 这非常像通才时代、或通才崛起的现在。当我们想一个能很扁平的团队，你仍想要在某些领域能很尖（spiky）的人。比如，显然一个会写代码的产品设计师，那很好。它让你真能跨很多不同领域。再说一次，一个超扁平的组织，当你戴很多不同帽子，那意味着每个人——如果你是通才，你默认能戴很多不同帽子。那帮我们维持这个想法：我们面前的机会能轻易扩张。每个人扮演巨大角色。他们不用等、不用请求许可。他们能去拿一块工作，因为就在那，他们至少能开个头，哪怕不是总能看到它做完。(01:39:34)：对我们来说，我觉得通才崛起会很重要。你总能用承包商或某领域超专业的代理来补充。这就是——回到 influencer 营销，你可能跟代理合作，而不是扩自己的 influencer 营销团队。你跟那的超专业团队合作。但我的营销团队全是通才。我们市场负责人最近在旧金山搞了场酷的无人机秀。我们在旧金山有 4000 人。市长来了，她造了整个项目、端到端自己管了整个项目，同时还管整个营销团队。所以是那种通才能玩所有不同角色、仍能超高影响力的想法。对我们，这也和我们说的另一个角色手牵手——player coach（球员兼教练）。传统的管理层就像经理管一堆人，那是他核心聚焦。(01:40:33)：我们所有人 leader 都是 player coach——他们仍自己做底层工作，也能指导教练身边的人。这个类比来自、这个 mindset 来自，我从体育界借来的，因为很多运动节奏极快。比如橄榄球，动得超快。所以你可能有教练在叫战术，但四分卫能根据看到的防守做最后调整。所以你想要场上能按需调整的球员，那样教练不用每件事都叫。他只是给你想跑的战术的大致意图，然后四分卫仍能调整。(01:41:13)：所以我们所有人 leader、我们的管理层，都是真能做那些调整的人。如果他们日常或每周看到不对的，他们在调那团队的优先级，而且他们自己仍在做工作。他们离得那么近，所以随时理解相对优先级是什么。所以这两点我觉得——当我想创始人，他们常想创新是“我们要在产品上创新或技术上创新”。我觉得今天每个创始人都有机会在组织设计上创新，那从想“我们今天想建什么类型的公司？”开始。什么意思？到管理层，我们招什么类型的 leader？到招具体角色和职能什么意思？所有那都是你用心、建一家你希望待很多很多年的公司的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing here is manager, there's no pure managers at Gamma and your plan is to not have people that are just managing the ideas. Everyone, even a manager is doing their own IC work.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是，经理——Gamma 没有纯经理，你的计划是不要有只管想法的人。每个人，甚至经理，都在做自己的 IC（个人贡献者）工作。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then the other piece of advice here is just generalists. People that can do a lot of stuff, and I hear this a lot on this podcast just like everyone is, there's no more just like you're a designer, that's all you're going to do. Designers need to build stuff, market stuff, write some PRDs probably.
turns.zh: 然后另一块建议是通才。能做很多事的人，我在这档播客总听到——就像大家一样，不再只是“你是设计师，你就只做设计”。设计师需要建东西、marketing、大概还要写点 PRD。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Just one thing to add is that's where we are at today. I think being adaptable means that certain things may evolve and change and how the player coach model evolves and maybe in certain functions or as the team scales, that's not going to be practical everywhere. I think the reality is you just have to know and be willing to adopt different frameworks over time and being honest with yourself with what's working, what's not. I think we're constantly trying to learn and evolve ourselves. I think we're doing it in a way that we don't believe it really has been done before, and so we have to kind of pave our own path over time.
turns.zh: 就加一点：那是我们今天的状态。我觉得能适应意味着某些事会演进、变化，player coach 模型怎么演进、也许在某些职能或团队扩时，那不会处处实用。现实是你只需知道、并愿意随时间采用不同框架，对自己诚实什么是管用、什么不。我觉得我们不断试图学、演进自己。我们做的方式是我们不觉得以前真有人这么干过，所以我们得随时间铺自己的路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Giving yourself an out when the time comes when you need to just hire managers.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。给自己在需要时真去招经理的时候留个退路。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: A year later when you invite me back, I'll say, "Yeah, this is what we learned."
turns.zh: 一年后你再邀我回来，我会说“对，这是我们学到的”.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that makes sense. That's probably going to happen. It's like people are like, "We don't need product managers." [inaudible 01:43:22] "I see. Maybe we do." Yeah, that makes sense. One last piece I want to talk about is you have this really cool quote that you shared on Twitter. " When you find someone exceptional, bet big on them." This is a big part of your philosophy is just bet big on the people that are doing super well. Just talk about what that looks like and why that's so important.
turns.zh: 对，说得通。那大概会发生。就像人们说“我们不需要产品经理”。[听不清 01:43:22]“我懂了。也许我们需要。”对，说得通。最后一块想聊的是你推特上分享的一句超酷的话：“当你发现一个出众的人，在他身上下大注（bet big）。”这是你哲学的一大块——就在做得超好的人身上下大注。讲讲那长什么样、为什么那么重要。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean this starts top of the funnel, which is you meet candidates, you decide who you actually hire. And so if you don't start with a high bar there, going back to what is the goal? The goal is to hit a hiring target versus maintaining a super high quality hiring bar. Those are different goals and I don't think we've ever kind of dropped our bar. And so then you bring somebody in that you think is exceptional, that brings something unique to the table, that can be a good teammate. When they're thriving, you just give them more and more resources. I think what you realize, another sports analogy is when you're on an A team for instance, or a team that you feel like is exceptional, A players want actually more playing time. You never see a star player that says "I actually want less playing time." (01:44:26): They want more time on the field, they want to actually go after the hardest problems. They want to be able to feel like they're making a huge impact. And so if you have fewer exceptional teammates where you can just throw almost anything at them and they'll figure it out, that feels for you as a team, just feels great because then they get what they find rewarding, which is the ability to go after hard hairy problems and to be able to come out through the other end feeling like they've accomplished something. And I think that for us has always been something that goes beyond just almost everything else. We give people a chance to really thrive in this environment and we try to nurture that as much as humanly possible every step of the way.
turns.zh: 有，我是说这从漏斗顶部开始——你见候选人、决定真招谁。所以如果你不在那起个高标准，回到目标是什么？目标是达成招聘指标、相对维持超高质的招聘标准。那是不同目标，我觉得我们从不降标准。所以你把你认为出众、能带来独特东西、能当好朋友的人招进来。当他们 thriving，你就给他们越来越多资源。我觉得你会意识到——另一个体育类比——当你在一支 A 队、或你觉得出众的队，A 级球员其实想要更多上场时间。你从没见过球星说“其实我想少上点场”。(01:44:26)：他们想要更多场上时间，想要去攻最难的问题。他们想要感觉自己在造成巨大影响。所以如果你有更少但出众的队友，你能把几乎任何东西扔给他们、他们会搞定，那对你作为团队感觉超好，因为他们得到他们觉得有回报的东西——去攻那些难而毛糙的问题、并能从另一端出来感觉自己成就了什么。我觉得对我们来说，那一直超越几乎其他一切。我们给人真在这个环境里 thriving 的机会，我们每一步都尽可能培育那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else around hiring that you think is really important or a big lesson you've learned or lesson you share that we haven't talked about yet?
turns.zh: 招聘周围还有没有什么是你觉得真重要、或你学到的大教训、或还没聊到的分享?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: I mean, there's some of these intangibles, which is for the founding team, does this feel like this could be your life's work? When you're pitching a potential candidate, does this feel like something where you're actually committed? The unfortunate side of a lot of what's happening in the AI world broadly is I think you're coming to learn which founders are sort of missionaries versus mercenaries. And many that were just chasing maybe just a big outcome, or something shiny, or something to feel good about themselves, they'll go off and then the company, I guess doesn't live on or maybe has to find a different way, a different path. (01:45:47): And so something I admire is you look at some of the founders, obviously before this sort of AI era, folks like Dylan or Melanie, Figma, Canva, Ivan at Notion, they've been doing this for over a decade now. They had many chances to just leave and sunset off into doing whatever they wanted to do, but they care so much about the mission, they've stuck it through. And I think when you're talking to candidates, candidates can kind of tell, is this something the founders even care about? And I think you're going to have a better chance of attracting true missionaries, people that want to build with you for the long haul, if it's authentic and it's something you actually care about.
turns.zh: 我是说有些无形的东西——对创始团队，这感觉能是你毕生的事业吗？当你 pitch 一个潜在候选人，这感觉像你真投入的事吗？AI 世界广泛发生的事里不幸的一面是，我觉得你会学到哪些创始人是 missionary（传教士）相对 mercenary（雇佣兵）。很多只是追也许一个大结果、或闪亮的东西、或让自己感觉好，他们会走掉，然后公司——我猜活不下去、或得找不同方式、不同路。(01:45:47)：所以我钦佩的是你看一些创始人——显然在这 AI 时代前——像 Dylan、Melanie（Figma）、Canva、Ivan（Notion），他们干这已经十多年了。他们有很多机会离开、去搞任何想搞的，但他们太在乎使命，坚持下来了。我觉得当你跟候选人聊，候选人能感觉到——创始人甚至在不在乎这事？我觉得如果它是真的、是你真在乎的，你更有机会吸引真 missionary、想长期跟你建的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I keep saying this. I feel like we could have at least five more hours of stuff to talk about. That'll be good content for when you come back and you're making a billion dollars a year. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, Grant, is there anything else that you think is important for people to hear? Any last, I don't know, lesson you want to double down on? Anything you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 噢老兄，我一直在说这个。我觉得我们至少还能聊五个小时。那会是你回来、一年赚十亿时好内容。在我们进入超激动的闪电轮（lightning round）之前，Grant，还有没有什么是你觉得重要、该让人听到的？任何最后的、我想再加倍的教训？想留给听众的?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, just going back to the original story of that was probably the ultimate low point. Having an investor that spent 20 minutes listening to my pitch, telling me that it was the worst thing, worst idea in the world. I think throughout the journey there's going to be those low moments. And when I think about being a founder and working a startup, you're honestly just trying to increase your luck surface area as much as possible. And for me, luck surface area has two dimensions. The first dimension is people. Who are you surrounding yourself with that share your same ambition, share the same values, same principles, and find those people and then give yourself enough time to prove that you guys can accomplish great things. I'm lucky to have two amazing co-founders. We've been working on this thing for five years. There's 0% chance we'd be where we are if I didn't have them. And we've had to overcome a lot. But I guess for us it's like creating that own luck over a long time horizon has been the only way that it's been possible.
turns.zh: 有，回到最初那个故事——那大概是终极低点。一个投资人花 20 分钟听我路演，告诉我那是世界上最糟的东西、最烂的想法。我觉得整段旅程会有那些低潮时刻。当我想做创始人、搞创业公司，你其实就在试图尽可能扩大你的“运气表面积”（luck surface area）。对我来说，运气表面积有两个维度。第一维是人。你身边围着什么人——和你有同样野心、同样价值观、同样原则，找到那些人，然后给自己足够时间去证明你们能成就大事。我很幸运有两个超棒的联合创始人。我们搞这事五年了。如果没他们，我们 0% 可能到今天这地步。我们克服了很多。但对我们来说，长期自己造运气，是唯一的办法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, it's clearly showing in the success you guys are having. Grant, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 对，那明显体现在你们正有的成功里。Grant，说完这个，我们到了超激动的闪电轮。准备好了吗?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yep. Yes.
turns.zh: 对。准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. I've got five questions for you. First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 好。我有五个问题给你。第一个，哪两三本书你最常推荐给别人?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, so I'll give one that's for pre-product market fit folks and the one post-product market fits.
turns.zh: 好，我给一个给 pre-PMF（产品市场契合前）的人，一个给 post-PMF 的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Pre-product market fit I would say is Shoe Dog, which is written by Phil Knight, founder of Nike. And he talks about two things. One, you should chase your sort of crazy ideas, but these should be ideas you're passionate about. He was an athlete, and so not surprisingly, he focused a lot about creating tools or shoes in this case for other athletes and was passionate about that. And the second thing he taught me was going back to the team thing, he surrounded himself with other people that were super passionate about athletics and shoes as well. And so the folks that he had as his initial startup crew were all that. (01:48:49): And I think that gives you a chance of overcoming a ton, where you're focused on problems you actually care about solving, and you're dealing with a team that shares the same ambition as you. Post-product market fit, there's a book called 7 Powers by Hamilton Helmer, where I think when you think about how to build a durable business, there's so much in there. I think there's a lot that you can kind of read and reread as you kind of evolve and hit new milestones yourself. And so much of that can be both tactical but also zooming out and thinking about what are the big picture strategic questions you as a founding team you need to be thinking about. So both are great.
turns.zh: pre-PMF 我会说是《Shoe Dog》，Nike 创始人 Phil Knight 写的。他讲两件事。一，你该追你疯狂的想法，但这些该是你有热情的。他是运动员，所以不意外，他很聚焦为其他运动员造工具或鞋、并对那有热情。他教我的第二件事回到团队——他围着其他对田径和鞋也超热情的人。所以他初始创业班底全是那样。(01:48:49)：我觉得那给你克服一堆的机会——你聚焦在你真在乎解的问题，你和一个共享你同样野心的团队共事。post-PMF 有本书叫《7 Powers》（Hamilton Helmer 写），当你想怎么建耐久生意，里面有太多。我觉得随着你演进、到自己达新里程碑，很多你能读、重读。那里很多既实操、也能拉远想“作为创始团队你需要想的大局战略问题是什么”。所以两本都超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hamilton was on the podcast, we'll link to that episode. I also love that book. Many people mention it. Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: Hamilton 上过播客，我们会链到那期。我也爱那本书。很多人提它。下一个问题，你最近有喜欢的电影或剧吗?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, The Lazarus Project is one, I'm a huge sucker for time travel and sci-fi, so this is one I just started watching. And for me, it has all the right ingredients for a fun show.
turns.zh: 有，《The Lazarus Project》是一个，我是时间旅行和科幻的超级粉，所以这是我刚开看的。对我，它有所有好看剧该有的配料。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a product you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 有最近发现、你真爱的产品吗?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mentioned this already, Voicepanel. So again, a full disclosure angel investor, but we've been using it and going back to kind of being a cheat code for folks that are starting to experiment a ton with different ideas, vibe coding, maybe some of these might get this into the hands of users, hear what they think about it. I think, and honestly can help speed up a lot of things and save you time from wasting time on the wrong ideas or ideas where there's no market.
turns.zh: 有，我已经提过，Voicepanel。再说一次，坦白我是天使投资人，但我们一直在用，回到——对开始大量实验不同想法、vibe coding、也许把这些交到用户手里、听他们想的人的“作弊码”（cheat code）。我觉得，老实说能帮加速很多事、省下你把时间浪费在错想法或没市场的想法上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a life motto that you often find yourself coming back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 有句人生格言你常回到的吗，工作 or 生活?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, so there's this Chinese idiom that my mom used to say, it's a [foreign language 01:50:24] which the translation is "A frog at the bottom of a well". And the story is like there's a frog at the bottom of the well. He looks up every night and he sees the world and he imagines he knows everything about the world. And then one day a bird comes along and describes all the things that he sees, the ocean, the mountains, and the frog realizes that what he sees is just such a limited part of the world and the bird asks, "Do you want to come join me?" And kind of see the rest of it. And so frog goes along. (01:50:54): And so for me, I came from a pretty modest childhood. My parents, we didn't have a whole lot and I think it would've been very easy to kind of have a very narrow lens on the world and be like, "Oh, this is what it is." But my mom never allowed me to do that. She always pulled me to dream much bigger to say, "Hey, the world is vast. It's your opportunity to seize it. You have to go out there, don't have a narrow view of what's possible. Always dream bigger." And so for me, that's always carried through and every time I feel like I'm thinking too little or too small, I try to zoom out and remind myself that there's much more out there to go after.
turns.zh: 有，有个我妈常说的中国成语，是[外语 01:50:24]翻译是“井底之蛙”。故事是有只青蛙在井底。他每晚抬头看世界，以为自己知道关于世界的一切。然后一天一只鸟飞来，描述它看到的一切——海洋、山脉——青蛙意识到他看到的只是世界极有限的一部分，鸟问“你想来跟我一起吗？”去看剩下的。(01:50:54)：对我来说，我来自相当普通/ modest 的童年。我父母没太多，我觉得很容易对世界有很窄的镜头、觉得“噢，就这样了”。但我妈从不允许我那样。她总拉我梦想更大，说“嘿，世界很大。是你的机会去抓住它。你得走出去，别对可能的事有窄视野。永远梦更大。”所以对我来说，那一直贯穿，每次我觉得自己想太小太少，我就试着拉远、提醒自己外面还有多得多要去追的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so good and so important and so valuable in today's world where so much more is possible. Just like, most of what limits people it feels like now is just, I don't know what idea I have. I don't know what to do. Now you could get things done so much quicker and so much more is possible. So that's such valuable thinking. Okay, final question. You help people present better. Your tools basically help people become better presenters. What's one tip you've learned or one tip you teach people to become better presenters that might be helpful to listeners?
turns.zh: 那太好了、太重要、在当下这世界太有价值——现在可能多得多。就像，限制大多数人的，感觉只是“我不知道我有什么想法。我不知道做什么”。现在你能快得多地把事做成，可能多得多。所以那思考太有价值。好，最后一个问题。你帮人呈现更好。你的工具基本帮人成为更好的演示者。你学到或教人的、让人成为更好演示者、可能对听众有用的一招是什么?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I'll go back to the consumer advertising concept, which is one idea at a time, this notion of you give them one egg, someone can catch it, give them too many eggs, they're going to drop it. So don't try to throw too many concepts all at once. Keep it simple. People will appreciate it. And so with every sort of presentation, break it down into the core concepts, try to make sure you're covering one at a time. And I think once you sort of see a through line there, then it becomes easy for it to package up into something that feels more cohesive.
turns.zh: 有，我回到消费广告概念——一次一个想法，那个“给他们一个鸡蛋、有人接得住，给太多鸡蛋、他们会掉”的概念。所以别试图一次扔太多概念。保持简单。人们会感激。所以每个演示，分解成核心概念，确保一次覆盖一个。我觉得一旦你看到一条 through line（主线），那它就容易打包成更 cohesive 的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Less is more, as they say.
turns.zh: 少即是多，如他们所说。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Grant, two final questions. Where can folks find you online? Where can they find Gamma? What should they know? Just plug anything you want and then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: Grant，最后两个问题。人们哪能线上找到你？哪能找到 Gamma？该知道什么？随便 plug 任何你想的，然后听众怎么帮你?

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Yeah, so you can find me on both Twitter and LinkedIn, DM's open. I honestly hear just knowing how hard the journey is in general, whether just thinking about a startup idea or you're deep into startup land, I want to be hopefully helpful. I'm going to be hopefully your biggest cheerleader, so let me know how I can help. And then for us, we're always looking for feedback. So if you're trying Gamma, it's falling short of your expectations, let us know. We'd love to help in terms of just trying to make it better. And yeah, really appreciate all the feedback and support along the way.
turns.zh: 好，你能在 Twitter 和 LinkedIn 上找到我，DM 开放。老实说，光是知道这旅程多难——无论是想个创业想法、还是深陷创业，我想尽量有用。我想当你的头号啦啦队长，所以让我知道怎么帮你。对我们来说，我们总在找反馈。所以如果你在试 Gamma、它没达到你预期，告诉我们。我们想在“让它更好”上帮忙。一路上真的感激所有反馈和支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Grant, this was awesome. I really appreciate you making time. I know you're trying to build a crazy fast-growing startup with a lot going on, so I really appreciate you making time for this.
turns.zh: Grant，这超棒。我真感激你抽时间。我知道你在搞一个疯涨的创业公司、一堆事，所以我真感激你抽时间做这个。

turns.speaker: Grant Lee
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. It's been a blast.
turns.zh: 谢谢，Lenny。这超好玩。

turns.en: It's been a blast for me too. Bye everyone. (01:53:29): Thank you so much for listening.
